text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The deadline passed Tuesday for the Trump administration to ask the Supreme Court to reconsider its rejection of the president’s birthright citizenship restrictions, with no new filing on the docket.

President Donald Trump vowed to seek a rehearing shortly after the opinion handed him a loss on a signature issue, but by Tuesday the 25-day window had elapsed with no new activity.

A petition would face long odds: The court has not agreed to rehear an argued case in more than 50 years.

The high court’s 6-3 decision in June struck down Trump’s executive order that would have denied automatic citizenship to children born in the United States whose parents are in the U.S. illegally or temporarily.

The Republican president’s restrictions on birthright citizenship had been blocked by several lower courts before reaching the justices, and they did not take effect anywhere in the U.S.

Still, three justices — Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch and Clarence Thomas – would have upheld them. A fourth justice, Brett Kavanaugh, found the Constitution wouldn’t block the president’s plan, though he found it did violate a federal law.

A week after the decision came down, Trump said in a social media post he would “be asking for a Rehearing by the United States Supreme Court, IMMEDIATELY.”

The White House and Justice Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.

The last time the Supreme Court granted any petition to change an opinion was in 1965, and the last time it reversed a decision was almost a decade earlier, in a case from 1956, said Aaron-Andrew Bruhl, a law professor at William & Mary Law School.

The bar to grant a petition for rehearing is high. It would require at least one justice who ruled against Trump to change their mind and a majority of the court would have to agree, Bruhl said.

text:
AUGUSTA — The three candidates hoping to be Maine’s next governor offer different perspectives on how — or whether — they would cooperate with federal immigration agents if elected.

On Nov. 3, Maine voters will decide whether Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles or independent Rick Bennett will lead the state for the next four years.

Pingree, a former Maine House speaker, said she supports new state laws taking effect this week that restrict local law enforcement, schools, libraries and those who work in other public spaces from cooperating with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

“I’ve heard a lot of concern from people across Maine who want to see how the governor, how the state, how the attorney general can better protect people in the state of Maine,” she said. “People all over the state, especially in Biddeford, are feeling unsafe in a community that for many years has always felt very safe.”

The fear in Biddeford follows the July 13 shooting and killing of Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, 25, who was shot by an ICE agent while on his way to work. An investigation is ongoing, but federal officials have confirmed that Guerrero was not the intended target of the immigration enforcement action.

Charles, an attorney, lobbyist and former Naval Intelligence Officer, said in a statement that his “top priority will be the public safety of all of Maine residents.”

“As governor, I will work with federal law enforcement on violent and repeat offenders, but there are limits,” he said. “As governor, I will enforce all state laws.”

Independent Rick Bennett, a state senator and former Republican, voted in favor of the new state laws restricting cooperation with ICE. As governor, he said he would work with the federal government “to protect real public safety” but does not support what he views as unnecessary interference.

“There is a big difference between lawful cooperation and turning state and local systems into extensions of fear-driven federal enforcement,” he said. “Our immigrant and refugee neighbors are part of Maine, and they should not be forced to live in fear because Washington politicians want to score points.”

Pingree said while other states have tried to pass laws to require agents to remove masks, wear body cameras and show identification, she would look to work with other state leaders.

“I think it’s about working with other governors across the country, attorneys general, to actually hold ICE accountable,” she said.

She said she would also work with the state’s congressional delegation — she is the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-1st District) — to try to better regulate ICE operations in the states.

In January, ICE launched “Operation Catch of the Day,” which is how the federal government described its goal to arrest the “worst of the worst” in Maine. The agents picked up nearly 200 people, only 11 of whom had a criminal record, according to the Bangor Daily News.

When it comes to the Guerrero shooting earlier this month, Charles called for “full accountability and high standards” as the investigation continues.

“Law enforcement must follow the law, just as citizens must,” Charles said. “My view is to support legal immigration and oppose illegal immigration and especially prioritize the immediate removal of all criminal aliens to improve public safety.”

Bennett called for a “full and transparent” investigation that includes an examination of whether the agent involved in the Biddeford shooting followed protocol and what steps can be taken to prevent these types of incidents.

“I am deeply troubled by the fear the ongoing presence of ICE has sent through immigrant families across Maine,” he said. “Something is very wrong when people who have built their lives here wonder whether they can safely leave their homes for work, drop their children off at childcare or schools, or go out to buy groceries for their family.”

Pingree does not think ICE in its current form can be reformed but acknowledges that the states do need help from the federal government in enforcing immigration laws.

“We used to have sane Customs and Border Patrol, we used to have sane enforcement of our immigration laws,” she said. “People weren’t being shot in the street. People who were here legally were not being harassed on their way to work.”

Charles, who has emphasized lowering crime rates and tackling substance use disorder, said his focus will be on public safety.

“Our state should be welcoming to anyone who wants to live here, but public safety must be our top priority, and it will be mine,” he said.

Bennett said he’s not focused on whether ICE can be reformed or must be scrapped, but rather on how it does its job.

“The test should be simple: does the system uphold the law without trampling basic rights and terrorizing communities?” he said. “If it does not, then it needs to change.”

text:
Please be aware that this report includes content some people may find offensive.

As federal immigration agents surged throughout the U.S. for “Operation at Large” during the summer of 2025, some officials in Southern California referred to potential detainees using language widely considered to be racial slurs — describing Hispanic and Latino individuals as “wets” and “tonks” — body-camera footage and text messages cited in new court filings reveal.

“Just plug us in wherever you see some tonks and we’ll jump out,” one agent is quoted as saying, according to a transcript of body camera footage cited in court papers in the Central District of California.

That derogatory term, often used to describe migrants, reportedly references the sound made by slamming a heavy-duty flashlight or baton against an individual’s head, according to U.S. Border Patrol documents obtained by HuffPost in 2024.

During a separate incident in June of 2025 outside a Home Depot in Hollywood, body camera footage captured an agent saying quote: “There was a guy, I’m pretty sure he’s wet he was just sitting in that minivan.”

“Wet” is widely understood as a shorthand for “wetback” — a dehumanizing term for migrants who swim the Rio Grande from Mexico to the U.S.

Evidence also reveals agents repeatedly referring to potential arrestees as “possibles” based on their appearance, and an immigration official acknowledging in a deposition that an individual’s "Hispanic ethnicity” might make him more likely to be targeted for arrest, even as the Trump administration has repeatedly maintained officers are not engaged in racial profiling.

“We should not live in a country where people can be seized based on the color of their skin by masked men,” Annie Lai, a staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union and co-counsel on the case, told Scripps News.

“It's a kind of storm of circumstances that really make this a predictable outcome, not something that is accidental or that the administration needs to pay more attention to,” Lai added.

The new evidence comes as part of an ongoing lawsuit brought by a coalition of Southern California residents who claim they were the subject of racial profiling by immigration officials.

Last July, U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong granted a temporary restraining order blocking immigration officials from conducting arrests based only upon race, though that decision was ultimately stayed by the U.S. Supreme Court.

RELATED STORY | Supreme Court clears way to end TPS program protections for Haitians and other immigrants

In a brief opinion, Justice Brett Kavanaugh said federal law allows officers to “briefly detain” an individual for questioning if they have “a reasonable suspicion, based on specific articulable facts, that the person being questioned ... is an alien illegally in the United States.’”

The California judge later granted expedited discovery in the case, giving plaintiffs access to agents’ text messages and body camera footage. Lai told Scripps News she expected to uncover further evidence of officers’ wrongdoing, especially as attorneys wait for a ruling on whether immigration agents must turn over their personal devices in addition to government ones.

The new evidence was accompanied by a motion asking the judge to impose a preliminary injunction blocking immigration officials from engaging in racial profiling. Attorneys argue it “flatly disproves the representations Defendants made about their operations” when they asked the Supreme Court to stay the initial block on the policy, and reveals that “race is the predominant characteristic driving Defendants’ stops, and that Defendants’ ongoing stops — including of U.S. citizens — are neither brief nor unintrusive.”

MORE ON IMMIGRATION | New claims of human rights violations center on Texas ICE detention camp

Asked about the new disclosures, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told Scripps News in a statement that federal agents “are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage. Where is the media’s outrage for Angel families who lost a loved one to illegal alien crime?”

The official, who declined to speak on the record, did not answer questions about the new evidence or whether the agents who made those statements had been disciplined.

text:
Kentucky’s lone Democratic congressman, U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, joined two of his House colleagues to get a closer look at a Northern Kentucky jail holding federal immigration detainees Monday.

Speaking to reporters in Louisville Tuesday morning, McGarvey said the visit to the facility “as part of our ongoing and continuing oversight of what ICE is doing.” At the Campbell County Detention Center, he had joined U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, of Illinois, and U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore, of Wisconsin.

While privacy release forms prevented him from publicly sharing specific situations he heard during the visit Monday, McGarvey said “the stories are heartbreaking.”

“We talked to people yesterday, and they told us they’re not getting their medication. We talked to people yesterday who told us that they’re not getting the food they need. We talked to people who told us they’re not getting the medical care they need,” McGarvey said. He added with ICE getting billions in funding, “there is no excuse for them treating detainees this way.”

The Campbell County Detention Center is holding about 135 people on ICE’s behalf, according to data from Relevant Research. Throughout Kentucky, about 10 jails, including Campbell, are housing about 1,200 people for ICE.

In the Campbell jail, 118 of those people are in the non-criminal population.

McGarvey said the House members “went through the normal process” to request the visit, and “didn’t have any problems being granted access.” The House members asked questions and looked at facilities to “find out the conditions that people are really experiencing,” he added. McGarvey also said the visits are “very much part of our oversight duty as members of Congress.”

When asked if he would be part of more visits to jails holding people on behalf of ICE, McGarvey said: “We’ve done these before. We’ll do them again.”

Moore and Ramirez had said they were going to the facility to visit constituents housed there. Moore posted on X that she came to the facility “following reports of inhumane conditions and inadequate medical care of people in custody.” Ramirez said online that “Medical care in ICE detention is not negotiable!”

Campbell County Jailer James Daley, an elected Republican, did not return a voicemail left with his office seeking comment. However, Daley said according to LINK NKY he felt the visit was politically motivated and said claims about inadequate medical care were “an absolute lie.”

The League of Women Voters of Kentucky has been monitoring data regarding people being held by ICE in Kentucky jails, finding that more than 1,000 people are being held in Kentucky’s county jails for immigration reasons. An analysis from the group in March said that about three-fourths of those detained have no criminal record or pending charges.

Becky Jones, the first vice president of the League of Women Voters of Kentucky, said the group is concerned with what happens in “publicly funded jails and detention centers,” particularly those in Kentucky where ICE is holding people. The League is a nonpartisan advocacy organization that promotes informing the public.

In its review, the League continues to find more questions.

“The problem that we’re observing is that jail numbers don’t always match what the ICE numbers are, and so we have potentially people who are just disappearing from public record, and that’s concerning because, constitutionally, everybody deserves due process,” Jones said.

Jones added the League would encourage more congressional oversight visits in the future.

“What happens in jails affects everybody. If we cannot have public trust in what’s happening in our jails, everybody loses,” she said.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has extended its reach into North Carolina’s wilderness areas to find people suspected of living in the country illegally.

On Sunday, multiple arrests were made at Wilson Creek recreation area in Pisgah National Forest, which is managed by the U.S. Forest Service. The scenic river is about a 90-mile drive northwest from uptown Charlotte.

“ICE worked with USFS to arrest 13 illegal aliens, many of whom had criminal histories including DUI and illegal reentry – a felony,” ICE Public Information Officer Lindsay Williams told The Charlotte Observer in a July 28 news release.

“All of the illegal aliens have or will receive full due process. They will remain in ICE custody pending their removal or removal proceedings.”

The Caldwell County Sheriff’s Office reports it provided assistance during the operation, which included a checkpoint on a federal roadway. County officials note deputies routinely patrol the forest during the summer.

“Federal agents were responsible for the enforcement action, made 13 arrests, and transported those individuals from the scene. The Caldwell County Sheriff’s Office did not take custody of any of the individuals arrested,” Caldwell County Sheriff Kevin Bean said in a release posted to Facebook.

“Reports claiming that children were separated from their families during the operation are false. No children were taken from their families during this enforcement action.”

Wilson Creek is a 49,000-acre wilderness area where visitors can camp, kayak, hunt, fish and hike, according to the Caldwell Chamber of Commerce. Much of the waterway is within the Pisgah National Forest and extends more than 20 miles through the Blue Ridge Mountains, the chamber says.

ICE has encouraged people living in the country illegally to use the CBP Home App to get “$2,600 and a free flight to self-deport.”

text:
San Diego, CA – Today, Rep. Scott Peters convened business, labor, and community leaders to urge the Trump Administration to process Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) renewal applications in a timely manner. Delays at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), which seem intentional and politically motivated, have slowed renewal processing time to almost double what it used to be.

“Nearly 9,000 DACA recipients call San Diego home. They work hard, pay taxes, and contribute tens of millions of dollars to our local economy every year. For many of them, the U.S. is the only home they’ve ever known,” Rep. Peters said. “I spoke out when Donald Trump attacked DACA the first time, but our work is not over. We need answers from this Administration about the never-ending delays at USCIS. How do they plan to address the backlog they created? Are DACA recipients being detained because of this lag?”

President Trump’s immigration policies(link is external) have impacted the cost of healthcare, groceries, rent, and electricity. This is in part due to the delays in renewals which threaten the livelihoods of legal immigrants and put undue stress on businesses who are faced with uncertainty as their valued employees await decisions about their status. In San Diego alone, Dreamers, including DACA recipients, contribute $968 million(link is external) annually to the local economy.

"Every day a DACA renewal sits in a backlog is a day a San Diego business risks losing one of its own employees," said Chris Cate, President & CEO, San Diego Regional Chamber of Commerce. "After more than a decade of temporary protections, it's time for Congress to deliver a permanent, bipartisan solution that gives Dreamers the stability they deserve and gives San Diego employers the certainty they need.”

“Delays in processing DACA renewals are inexcusable and negligent,” said Dr. Arcela Nunez-Alvarez, Co-Founder and Co-Director, Universidad Popular. “These delays expose applicants to unnecessary suffering, including loss of work authorization, income, health coverage, and educational opportunities, and most importantly, loss of immigration protection. The delays create an adverse domino effect, increasing vulnerability for applicants and their families.”

“For a small business barely making payroll, DACA renewal delays mean shorter hours, slower service, lost revenue, and thousands of dollars in turnover costs – money that should be going to wages, growth, and this community,” said Trevor Moore, Vice President, Cush Enterprises. “DACA recipients have done everything by the book their entire lives. They register with the federal government and ask permission to keep working and paying taxes. Our economy is nothing without the effort and loyalty of these people.”

"For 18 months, this Administration’s chaotic, capricious, and arbitrary approach to immigration enforcement has been fundamentally about sowing fear and disrupting our communities,” said Carol Kim, Executive Secretary-Treasurer, San Diego and Imperial Counties Labor Council. “It also disrupts the ability of anyone to do business and reliably work, not just the workers who are targeted, but every working person whose specific tasks or projects are derailed by disappearing coworkers, disappearing funding, and disappearing basic government functions. Every American who expects that work to come through pays the price, too.”

DACA must be renewed every two years, and work authorizations cannot be renewed until DACA status is renewed. Rep. Scott Peters’ office is seeing the highest volume of immigration casework requests during his time in Congress, driven by these mounting delays which affect our community and economy.

A livestreamed recording of the press conference can be viewed here(link is external). Additional photos from the event, courtesy of the office of Rep. Scott Peters, can be viewed here(link is external).

text:
Today, Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07) joined Congressman Joaquin Castro (TX-20) and members of the House Democratic Women's Caucus (DWC) at a press conference with FWD.US and Families Belong Together, following their visit to the Dilley Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Detention Center. The oversight visit follows reports of inhumane treatment of children and families at the facility.

Congresswoman Fletcher’s press conference remarks as delivered:

Thanks so much, Congresswoman Ansari, and I join you in thanks for Congressman Castro and his entire team that have welcomed all of us to San Antonio and taken us to Dilley today. I am from just down the road, I'm Lizzie Fletcher from Houston, and am really grateful for the opportunity to be here today to witness myself what is happening in the great state of Texas and in the United States of America. And every American really needs to know what we saw at Dilley today and what we are seeing happening unfold in streets across this country, and so I'm grateful to everyone who's here, who's sharing this information. I’m grateful to FWD.US for the incredible work that they're doing to make sure that people don't look away from what we are seeing happening, and both of my colleagues have used the word, that if I had to have one takeaway from today, and one word, it is trauma.

The United States government is traumatizing individuals that it has in detention. I spent a lot of time today talking with some of the adults who were there, because there are families as well as a group of women who are detained at Dilley, and I spoke with women who've been there for eight months, who were picked up off the street while they were coming home from exercising. They had no idea why they were being picked up. They had no idea where they were going, and they have very little, if any, contact with anyone outside. They don't know what's happening with their asylum case. They don't know how long they'll be there. They don't know what's going to happen to them when they get out, and they're not getting any answers. They're not getting any information, and they're not getting any help, except from the people who are working so hard to share their stories and make sure that Americans know that this cannot go on. It cannot go on in our names. And what we see is these individual cases of trauma for the children and the families. But this immigration enforcement regime, ICE, and the Trump Administration are creating trauma not only for individuals, but they are terrorizing our communities, and they are creating trauma across our communities. And that's certainly true at my home in Houston, where, as all of you know, we recently saw ICE pursue someone who was not the target of an investigation, in unmarked vehicles, with plainclothes officers, trying to stop Lorenzo Araujo and detain the three men who were with him in his van after they shot and killed him in the street.

People in Houston are outraged, but they're also traumatized. This is a national trauma, and that's why people need to know what's happening, and people need to speak up and speak out wherever they are because this is being done in our names. This is being done by the United States government, and I think for most Americans, it is unimaginable, but it is also something, as Congressman Castro said, that has been hidden. It's been hidden because we are not getting information. This Congress is not conducting the oversight that it should be. That's why I'm so grateful to Congressman Castro and to the DWC for making sure that we are doing the oversight work that the majority in Congress is refusing to do, and we need to make sure that people across the country know, as Congresswoman Ansari said, by definition, no one at Dilley has a criminal record.

Americans are being lied to about what this administration is doing, who it's detaining, what's happening when it takes them into detention. They're not being honest with the people about how, and why, and what they are doing, and it has to stop. It absolutely has to stop. The detention that we see in Dilley and the trauma that we see in our communities, it doesn't serve the interests of the American people. It doesn't meet our values and our aspirations for who we are. I know that this is not who we are, and we all need to stand up in this moment to stop it. So again, I'm grateful to be with all these incredible fighters who are here, including my friend, and classmate, and colleague, an incredible fighter here from Boston, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley.

Texas holds the largest detained population of any state, averaging approximately 13,400 people per day in ICE custody as of mid-September 2025 across a rapidly expanding network of facilities. The ICE Detention Center in Dilley reopened in March 2025 after closing under the Biden Administration. Reports have revealed alarming conditions at Dilley, including poor food and water quality and serious health issues, including a measles outbreak and inadequate care for pregnant women.

Earlier this month, Congresswoman Fletcher joined 110 of her Democratic colleagues in an effort calling for the closure of the ICE Detention Center in Dilley. Since 2025, the Democratic Women’s Caucus has sent six oversight letters to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) calling out their mistreatment of pregnant detainees, insufficient healthcare accessibility, and violence against women.

To watch the press conference, click here.

title: Feds targeted Latinos more after Supreme Court's racial profiling decision, report says
description:
The League of United Latin American Citizens or LULAC, a Latino civil rights organization, found that court-sanctioned racial profiling has contributed to the disproportionate targeting of Latinos regardless of their immigration status.
Citing a recent UCLA study, LULAC said from January to October, federal immigration agents arrested more than 187,000 Latinos and deported more than 126,000.
“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the spokesperson wrote.
The indiscriminate immigration raids that terrorized Latino communities appeared to have worsened after the Supreme Court’s 6-3 decision in September, according to LULAC’s report.
But once the injunction lifted, federal immigration agents descended once more on Latino communities, even stopping U.S. citizens, according to LULAC.
text:
By almost every measure, Latino communities are bearing the brunt of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, according to a new report.

The League of United Latin American Citizens or LULAC, a Latino civil rights organization, found that court-sanctioned racial profiling has contributed to the disproportionate targeting of Latinos regardless of their immigration status.

“The impact of mass deportation is falling on Latinos as an ethnic group, not on undocumented immigrants as a legal category,” the report read in part. “U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, work-authorized immigrants, and multi-generational American families are absorbing measurable harm: economic, physical, and civic.”

Although other immigrant groups have been targeted, LULAC found that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have mostly focused on immigrants from Latin America, particularly workers with no criminal history, who are also more likely to face violence or be placed in detention centers with substandard conditions.

Citing a recent UCLA study, LULAC said from January to October, federal immigration agents arrested more than 187,000 Latinos and deported more than 126,000.

Latino arrests also jumped from under 3,900 to nearly 6,000 after Stephen Miller, White House senior advisor and chief architect of President Trump’s immigration policy, set a new goal of arresting 3,000 undocumented people a day.

In an email response to The Times, a spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security rejected the report’s findings.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the spokesperson wrote. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S.—NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

“Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” the spokesperson added. “The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices.”

LULAC’s report comes amid recent court filings claiming that federal immigration agents were caught on body camera footage and in text messages using racial slurs when referring to Latinos.

Additionally, Congress recently approved nearly $70 billion in immigration enforcement funding to cover the rest of Trump’s term with at least $38 billion to go to ICE and $26 billion to Customs and Border Protection.

LULAC said in putting the report together it reviewed public data and published studies to provide a fact sheet that paints a broader picture about the impact mass deportations are having on Latinos.

“The people being removed are disproportionately working-age, employed and without criminal records — the demographic core of the workforce in construction, hospitality, agriculture, food processing, and care work,” the report read.

As of July 11, more than 65,000 people were being held in detention and about 70% of the population had no criminal convictions, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a data gathering organization.

ICE detention data show that about 40% of detainees were being held for civil immigration violations including visa overstays and work visa violations.

Unless previously deported, living in the country illegally is considered a civil violation rather than a crime and carries penalties such as arrests, fines and deportation proceedings.

The indiscriminate immigration raids that terrorized Latino communities appeared to have worsened after the Supreme Court’s 6-3 decision in September, according to LULAC’s report.

The Supreme Court justices overturned a district court injunction that barred immigration agents in Los Angeles from roving around Home Depots and car washes, stopping brown-skinned, Spanish-speaking day laborers and others from arrest on immigration charges.

But once the injunction lifted, federal immigration agents descended once more on Latino communities, even stopping U.S. citizens, according to LULAC.

This month, the American Civil Liberties Union reviewed more than 1,200 enforcement incidents across eight states, identifying 155 U.S. citizens who were detained, targeted, or experienced law enforcement misconduct, and 437 incidents involving likely racial profiling. It also identified 214 children affected, including 32 Americans.

LULAC said the immigration raids had an economic impact. Citing a recent UCLA study, it said small business and Latino entrepreneurs in Los Angeles County saw foot traffic drop significantly, losing millions in potential revenue in June 2025.

A spokesperson for LULAC could not immediately be reached for comment.

text:
Five Democratic members of Congress and a pediatrician described conditions at the Dilley Immigration Processing Center as “child abuse” Tuesday after touring the facility. They called for the immediate release of detained families and the center’s closure.

CoreCivic operates the center, about 70 miles southwest of San Antonio. Dilley is the nation’s only operating ICE detention facility for families. Facility officials told the delegation that it held more than 500 people, including 112 children as young as 2 months.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-San Antonio, toured Dilley with Democratic Reps. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, Yassamin Ansari of Arizona, Lizzie Fletcher of Houston and Luz Rivas of California, all members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus.

After the tour, which was limited to two hours, the group issued a demand: “Free the children now.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Rep. Yassamin Ansari (@repyassansari)

They later held a news conference in San Antonio with Dr. Anita K. Patel, a pediatric critical-care physician, and representatives of FWD.us, an immigration and criminal justice advocacy organization, and Families Belong Together.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"I am here today to warn about an ongoing and imminent crisis just two hours down the road," Patel said. "We know unequivocally that children who are detained in ICE facilities are experiencing severe, predictable and lasting harm."

Pressley said facility officials told the delegation that Dilley held 84 families and four pregnant women.

"No child should be in jail," she said. "If a cage is gilded, it is still a cage, and they should not be there."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

During Castro’s May 26 inspection, Dilley held 345 people, including 97 children, according to his office. By Tuesday, those numbers had risen to 539 people and 112 children.

Castro attributed the increase to the Trump administration's recent surge in immigration arrests.

"Every single day that a child spends in Dilley, they are traumatized," Castro said.

Fletcher said the facility also housed a group of adult women. Pressley said officials described those being detained as "low-level non-criminals."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The members of Congress said they were only allowed to interview one child — a 16-year-old San Antonio girl being held with her father. Castro said the teenager told the delegation she was on her way to church with a friend when immigration officials detained her. According to Castro, authorities told her father she would be transferred out of state unless he came to pick her up. When he arrived, he was also detained, and the two were later transferred to the Dilley facility.

She also told the lawmakers that during her initial two-day detention at the San Antonio Processing Center at Crosspoint, a camera was pointed toward an area detainees used as a restroom, Castro said.

The delegation did not tour the San Antonio facility Tuesday, and the Express-News could not independently verify the allegation.

The lawmakers said trauma was the dominant theme of what they witnessed and heard during the visit. Castro said some children appeared expressionless, while others cried, clung to their parents or pleaded to leave. Parents, he said, appeared distraught and uncertain about the status of their immigration cases.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Fletcher said she spoke with women who had been detained for as long as eight months. They told her they had little contact with people outside the facility and did not understand the status of their asylum cases or how much longer they would remain in custody.

"The United States government is traumatizing individuals that it has in detention," Fletcher said.

Patel accompanied the lawmakers during the tour and spoke about the physical and psychological effects detention can have on children. She said her advocacy was inspired by the case of Juan Nicolás, a 2-month-old boy who had been held with his mother at Dilley for nearly a month.

"I got into this fight because of a baby — a 2-month-old baby, Juan Nicolás," Patel said. "I have made it my mission to shed light on what is happening inside Dilley."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Juan Nicolás was taken to a hospital in February after developing respiratory problems and was initially diagnosed with bronchitis. Patel said doctors later determined he had respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV.

Later that month, Immigration officials deported the infant, his mother and other family members to Mexico.

At the time, the Department of Homeland Security said the infant was taken to a hospital in Pearsall for a "precautionary evaluation" after showing symptoms of a respiratory infection. The agency said he was in stable condition, was not admitted and continued to receive medical monitoring after returning to Dilley.

Patel pointed to the American Academy of Pediatrics' longstanding opposition to detaining immigrant children, saying the medical evidence documenting the harm caused by detention is "incontrovertible."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The academy has called for ending the detention of immigrant families and children and has said DHS facilities do not meet basic residential-care standards for children.

Lawmakers also described accounts of delayed medical care, limited access to attorneys and inadequate information about immigration proceedings. The Express-News could not independently verify those accounts. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately respond Tuesday to questions submitted through the Department of Homeland Security.

Castro said he spoke with a woman whose heart condition worsened while she was detained. According to Castro, she underwent a medical procedure but did not receive the recommended follow-up care or prescribed medication.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Pressley said she met a 30-year-old delivery driver who told lawmakers she had lived in the United States since she was 4. The mother of two said immigration officers detained her while she was delivering packages and that her children were now living with a former partner she accused of abusing her. According to Pressley, the former partner was released on a $150 bond after allegedly assaulting her, while the woman was told she would have to pay a $9,000 bond to be released from immigration detention.

The woman has not been publicly identified, and the Express-News could not independently verify her account, immigration status or the reported bond amounts.

The delegation also criticized what it described as increasing restrictions on congressional oversight.

Castro said he was disappointed that the director of ICE’s San Antonio field office had stopped attending recent inspections. Congress funds the immigration detention system, and federal law protects lawmakers’ access to DHS detention facilities for oversight visits, the lawmakers said. They are not permitted to take photographs or video during their inspection.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Tuesday's visit marked Castro's seventh inspection of the Dilley facility this year, according to his office.

Lawmakers said they saw Texas National Guard members at the facility and were told that about two dozen were working there. The Guard members’ duties were not immediately clear.

The delegation also questioned how ICE and CoreCivic provide information about legal rights to families who speak different languages. Castro said a digital screen in the intake area repeatedly displayed legal information in a language he believed might be Chinese. A detained woman told the delegation that the language did not change during the nine hours she spent in the intake room, he said.

Facility officials said the languages rotate on the screen. Castro said he encountered a similar issue during a previous visit when he tested a hotline intended for detainees to report sexual abuse.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Tuesday's inspection came less than two weeks after Castro and 110 other House Democrats urged Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to terminate CoreCivic's contract, close the Dilley facility and end family detention.

The lawmakers sent the letter July 15, and Castro’s office announced it publicly the following day. In it, they alleged children and parents held at Dilley had been subjected to contaminated food, unsafe drinking water, inadequate education, disrupted sleep and delayed or denied medical care.

The letter cited accounts from current and former detainees, attorneys, journalists and advocacy organizations.

"Parents describe horrendous conditions at Dilley, leading to severe depression, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation amongst their children," the lawmakers wrote.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The lawmakers also alleged DHS routinely holds children beyond the general 20-day limit established under the Flores Settlement Agreement, which governs the treatment of minors in immigration custody.

Citing federal court filings from February and March, they said children at Dilley spent an average of about 57 days in custody, with a median stay of about 44 days. According to the filings, 92 children were held for 61 to 90 days, while another 80 remained in custody for more than 91 days.

The Express-News has previously reported on legal challenges to prolonged family detentions at Dilley. In April, U.S. District Judge Fred Biery ordered the release of a woman and her five children after they had been detained there for about 10 months.

In April, the Express-News reported that the Trump administration’s expanded detention policies were overwhelming San Antonio’s federal courts. At the time, more than 38,000 habeas corpus petitions challenging immigration detention had been filed nationwide since January 2025, including more than 7,600 in Texas.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Among those cases was one involving 5-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos and his father, who were being held at Dilley. A federal judge ordered their release, and Castro accompanied them home to Minnesota.

READ MORE: 'Traumatizing children': In scathing ruling, Texas judge orders 5-year-old boy, his dad be released

Castro also advocated for two Cambridge Elementary School students and their stepmother after ICE agents detained them while they walked to an Alamo Heights school bus stop. The family spent about two weeks at Dilley before a federal judge ordered their release.

Dilley's reopening is part of the Trump administration's broader immigration crackdown, which has expanded arrests, increased detention and revived large-scale family detention. The Biden administration ended family detention in 2021.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

As of July 11, ICE was holding 65,765 people in detention, up from 60,311 on April 4, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a research organization that analyzes federal immigration data. Administration officials have said the expanded use of detention is necessary to enforce immigration law and ensure immigrants appear for court proceedings.

Attorneys and immigrant-rights organizations argue that prolonged detention without access to bond hearings violates immigrants' due process rights.

Dilley can house about 2,400 people. From late 2021 until ICE ended its funding on Aug. 9, 2024, the facility held single adults.

In March 2025, CoreCivic announced it had reached an agreement with ICE and the city of Dilley to resume family detention. The center began receiving families the following month.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

CoreCivic operates the facility under an amended agreement between ICE and the city of Dilley and leases the property from Target Hospitality. The agreement runs through March 2030, and CoreCivic has projected the facility could generate about $180 million in annual revenue once fully activated.

Contract documents obtained by the Houston Chronicle show the federal government pays about $15.6 million a month to operate Dilley, including roughly $2.5 million for medical services, regardless of how many people are detained.

CoreCivic has said the facility complies with federal detention standards, provides pediatric care and is closely monitored by government officials.

The company also says it does not decide who is detained or how long people remain there.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Castro argued that private operation creates a financial incentive to continue detaining families.

title: How Akron-Canton Airport is becoming a major hub for deportations

An Eastern Air flight that landed at the Akron-Canton Airport in the past week had initially filed a flight plan to Springfield.

text:
Akron-Canton Airport has become a hub for charter flights transporting and deporting immigrants.

The flights are operated by Eastern Air Express for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

An airport spokeswoman stated the airport cannot legally restrict access to federally chartered aircraft.

Advocacy groups are monitoring the flights and have planned protests at the airport.

This story has been updated.

Akron-Canton Airport has become a major hub for an airline charter company that conducts immigrant transportation and deportations.

More than 130 chartered Boeing 737 flights operated by Eastern Air Express have landed at Akron-Canton since April 20, sometimes to pick up people in restraints who have disembarked from a prison bus or unmarked vans. Some of the planes are serviced and then wait several hours or a few days to be dispatched to another airport that often is adjacent to or near a federal detention facility.

Eastern Air Express is one of several charter companies participating in a network of Homeland Security transfers and deportations for immigrants apprehended by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, according to a variety of news stories and government websites.

A private company at the north end of the airport, identified by airport officials as AVFlight, services the Eastern Air Express planes and provides access to the tarmac for prison buses and vans. An email and a phone message to AVFlight on July 24 were not returned.

Eastern Air Express is part of Eastern Airlines, headquartered in Kansas City.

From a vantage point on West Airport Drive and looking beyond a chain link fence, one can see mostly Black and brown detainees who appear to be cuffed and shackled disembarking from buses and vans, checked by guards and then instructed to climb the stairs to the plane, one at a time.

Most planes can be tracked online at FlightAware.com, though a few of the Eastern Air flights have been blocked from public view.

On July 21, detainees from two buses, one with the markings of Transcor America and the other unmarked, boarded an Eastern Air Boeing 737 with the tail number N668CP, which departed in mid-morning for Richmond, Virginia. Their hands were bound and hanging at their waists. Some wore white t-shirts and gray pants, though many were in street clothes.

Transcor is a subsidiary of CoreCivic, a private prison company with a prison in Youngstown that last year announced an expansion shortly after Donald Trump’s inauguration to accommodate immigrant detentions. A CoreCivic official declined to discuss transportation of detainees who might have gone to Akron-Canton.

The airport activity comes at the same time that temporary protective status ends for Haitian immigrants, as ordered by the president. Trump targeted Springfield, Ohio, in the 2024 presidential debate with untruths about Haitians living there. Thousands of Haitians have found work in the Springfield area after being encouraged by local employers and a network of immigrant advocates, mostly led by clergy, have organized to resist.

An Eastern Air flight that landed at the Akron-Canton Airport in the past week had initially filed a flight plan to Springfield.

The activity at Akron-Canton’s buildings 36-41 on West Airport Drive varies from day to day. On most days, there is one Eastern Air plane, sometimes two.

On July 22, a black transport van with Ohio government plates and an open door was at the AVFlight location. Nearby, at the foot of the stairs to Eastern Air jet N808TJ were six people in matching uniforms and ball caps talking with three men in street clothes.

The plane and the van departed shortly afterward, with the plane destined for Bedford, Massachusetts, a hotly contested deportation site that has drawn the Massachusetts governor into protests.

On July 19, an Eastern Air jet made a direct flight to Akron-Canton from Tapachula International Airport near the Mexico-Guatemala border, non-stop, according to the FlightAware online tracking system. Tapachula has become a primary drop-off point for U.S. deportations.

Homeland Security operations at Akron-Canton temporary, airport spokeswoman says

Building 41 still bears the name of Ultimate Jet Charters, a company that went out of business in 2025, according to airport officials. Ultimate Jet became the subject of national news in 2022 when it provided the planes used by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to fly about 50 newly arrived immigrants to Martha’s Vineyard, where former president Barack Obama owns a home.

The appearance of flights out of Akron-Canton occurred immediately after the Youngstown-Warren Regional Airport closed its runways to large planes. The airport has been in line for major runway improvements for several years and this summer is undergoing reconstruction of runway surfaces.

It's unclear why Akron-Canton was chosen as a site for the flights.

Lisa Dalpiaz, a spokeswoman for the Akron-Canton Airport, said Homeland Security operations at the airport are expected to be temporary, but she did not know how long. She also said the airport only tracks plane landings and takeoffs for billing purposes and has no knowledge of how many people may be on the planes.

She said that as a public airport, “We cannot legally restrict access to [Akron-Canton] for public or private aircraft operations, including aircraft chartered for federal government purposes.”

Asked if the airport might pursue Eastern Air to become a more permanent operator, she said: “After AVFlight’s temporary arrangement, [Akron-Canton] has no plans to pursue Eastern Air as the airline does not align with our strategic priorities. Our focus remains on strengthening relationships with airline partners that meet the Airport's strategic objectives and provide reliable, long-term value for travelers and the region.”

According to the Western Reserve Port Authority, which oversees Youngstown-Warren, about $21 million in improvements to the main runway and taxiways are occurring now and likely to be completed in the next few months. An email to the airport authority seeking a more definitive completion date was not immediately answered.

The Youngstown airport previously served as Ohio’s most active immigration and customs transfer portal, according to independent ICE monitoring organizations that actively track flights on publicly available websites.

The Youngstown-Warren airport is in a rural area eight miles from the Youngstown CoreCivic prison. CoreCivic announced early in the administration of Donald J. Trump that it was expanding in Youngstown to accommodate anticipated growth in immigrant arrests. In addition, the Mahoning County sheriff in Youngstown and the Geauga County sheriff east of Cleveland have signed agreements to house immigrant arrestees.

A collaborative news documentary produced by 9News KUSA in Denver and aired July 17, ICE AIR: Inside America’s Secret Deportation Network, names Youngstown as a key hub and follows the movement of one Eastern Air Express Boeing 737 with the call sign “Tyson 57.”

After the improvement project began at Youngstown, Tyson 57 became a regular at Akron-Canton – at least 60 visits.

Three independent ICE tracking groups have identified Akron-Canton as a second-tier hub for deportation flights.

Protesters targeting Akron-Canton, other airports nationwide with ICE activity

In Northeast Ohio, the Ohio Immigrant Alliance has been monitoring flights from Youngstown and Akron-Canton for several months as well as preparing for increased arrests. The group is planning a protest at the Lauby Road entrance to the Akron-Canton Airport from 10 a.m. to noon Aug 1.

In Bedford, Massachusetts, an immigrant advocacy group has been tracking flights from Youngstown and Akron-Canton to Bedford’s Hanscom Field for more than a year, picketing weekly, according to news reports. They called on local and state officials to bring a stop to the flights.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey wrote then Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem demanding that Hanscom field no longer be used for the transportation of people detained by ICE.

An airport advisory commission last week heard an extensive report from the immigrant advocates who had been photographing Eastern Air activity for more than a year with estimates as to how many people were boarded on planes that they were able to observe.

Advocates are now calling for live camera surveillance, similar to livestreams installed at the Seattle airport following protests there.

Doug Oplinger is a retired reporter and editor for the Akron Beacon Journal. He continues to write and report on Ohio issues and designs and conducts community conversations on current issues. He can be emailed at oplingerdoug@gmail.com

text:
A federal judge has ordered the release of a witness to the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by federal immigration officers during a traffic stop in Houston.

U.S. District Judge Keith P. Ellison issued the order releasing Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego on Monday, one week after blocking the federal government from deporting him.

Rojas Pliego, who is currently being held at the Montgomery ICE Processing Center in Conroe, Texas, was on his way to work on July 7 when federal immigration officers stopped the vehicle in which he was a passenger. ICE officers fired shots at the vehicle, killing the driver, Salgado Araujo.

Since the shooting, Rojas Pliego has been in custody "without an individualized bond determination."

“Given the severity of this ongoing unconstitutional deprivation of Petitioner’s liberty, the Court concludes that immediate release from custody is required,” Judge Ellison wrote in his order.

ICE said in a statement that Araujo "weaponized his vehicle" and tried to run over an officer during the stop, prompting the officer to fire their weapon "in self-defense."

"The driver was struck, and emergency services were immediately contacted. The driver was transported to the hospital, where he passed away from his injuries," ICE said.

Tirado Pantoja has been in the country since 1996 and has a son and stepdaughter who are both U.S. citizens. He does not have a criminal record, according to his habeas petition.

Judge Ellison ordered the government to release Rojas Pliego from custody within 48 hours.

title: 'Lawbreakers' or 'like us'? Study explores how partisans think about immigration
description:
The new Northwestern University study explores how Republicans and Democrats who help shape their party’s platforms understand and think about immigration status at a time of increasingly punitive immigration politics.
Topics discussed with interviewees included: their activism experience, overarching political views, their views and involvement in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections, views on immigration and views on miscellaneous types of law-breaking.
Yeh discusses other timely findings from the study in this Q&A: Q: When did immigration restriction become a politically polarizing topic?
Violating immigration law is a civil — not criminal — offense.
Q: How does each political party view the role of migrants in the labor force?
text:
EVANSTON, Ill. — Interviews with political activists in Southern California showed stark differences in how migrants are viewed: either “like us” and deserving of rights, or lawbreakers undeserving of social belonging and benefits.

The new Northwestern University study explores how Republicans and Democrats who help shape their party’s platforms understand and think about immigration status at a time of increasingly punitive immigration politics.

“Meanings of migrant illegality” was published in May by the Cambridge University Press Law and Society Review. The study’s author is Jesse Yeh, a political sociologist and assistant professor of instruction in legal studies at Northwestern’s Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences.

Yeh conducted interviews between 2020-2021 with a multiracial group of 65 Democratic and Republican activists in Southern California’s Orange and San Bernardino counties, a rich context for studying party activist attitudes toward migrant lawbreaking. A liberal state, California is also the birthplace of the New Right and passed the anti-migrant legislation Proposition 187 in 1994.

Participants were recruited from local chapters of Democratic and Republican clubs and included officers of the county parties. Their median age was 56 and the average interview length was nearly two hours. Topics discussed with interviewees included: their activism experience, overarching political views, their views and involvement in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections, views on immigration and views on miscellaneous types of law-breaking.

The study found Republicans and Democrats have polarized views of undocumented migration but agree on preferred policy outcomes to address the issue.

Yeh discusses other timely findings from the study in this Q&A:

Q: When did immigration restriction become a politically polarizing topic?

A: Consensus over addressing immigration issues was largely bipartisan in the 1980s. Polarization started in the early 2000s when some states passed measures restricting immigrant rights.

Violating immigration law is a civil — not criminal — offense. Previously, the lack of due process for immigrants was justified on the grounds that detention and deportation were not conceived to be punishment. Both have become increasingly punitive, which raises new questions about what the extent of rights for immigrants should be.

Q: How does each political party view the role of migrants in the labor force?

A: The people I interviewed were not concerned with immigrants taking their jobs. What they did think about was whether immigrants deserve to have a job and benefits. Most spoke about prioritizing care for their own citizens before allowing immigrants to partake in public benefits.

Q: Why are some groups denied asylum and others expedited for citizenship?

A: Across party lines, I found a tremendous consensus in the way people think about undocumented immigrants. Rather than considering if an individual broke the law, they thought about a person’s imagined place in society and the economy. Those beliefs about the belonging of immigrants are often shaped by perceptions about socioeconomic status, race and ethnicity.

Q: How do members of each party view deportation?

A: My interview findings were consistent with recent polling. More Democrats lean toward amnesty for all immigrants, and more Republicans support zero tolerance and deportation. But what is most interesting is there is tremendous consensus among most people of both parties in wanting a pathway to citizenship for some people.

For example, one Republican respondent, John, a Southeast Asian businessman in his mid-40s, said legality was very important to him, but regarding policy he said, “We need to get them becoming citizens…And if they’re here illegally causing crime, they need to be gone.”

Likewise, a Democratic respondent, Danielle, a white retired attorney in her late 60s, said legality was not important to her because of the desperation that leads people to come here, but her preferred policy was similar to John’s. “There should be a path to citizenship for people who are here for whatever reason, and are good people, who are working and who are not breaking the law.”

Q: What do people frequently misunderstand about immigration law?

A: A big concern people have is not wanting to accept people as citizens who have committed a crime. But what makes someone a criminal is a capacious category. Are speeding or parking tickets criminal? What feels illegal to some people may not actually be breaking the law. Many people feel those who are affiliated with people thought to be gang-related are criminal, even if they have no record. This begs the question of what it means to not want people who are criminals to have citizenship.

It’s also important to know the distinctions of legal and illegal are arbitrarily created. “Legality” is often used as shorthand without defining what we mean when we use those categories. As the recent Temporary Protected Status Supreme Court case shows, the very same person can go from “legal” to “illegal” depending on the changes in the administration.

Q: What should lawmakers take from this study?

A: One insight for lawmakers is to consider how we define the boundaries of eligibility to become American.

Across party lines, people are supportive of young people brought here as children and eligible for DACA. Since many voters think upstanding young people have a lot to contribute to society, they believe it should be immaterial if they broke the law if they entered the U.S. as minors with adults.

When people talk about a pathway to citizenship, they often mean there should be amnesty for some members of the immigrant population. But the legal channel to come is tremendously narrow if someone doesn’t have a U.S. relative or can’t land a job before coming here.

Lawmakers can consider new ways to draw these boundaries, so they are less arbitrary, and so more immigrants who are poised to make positive contributions to society will have a legal path to citizenship.

text:
Beata Siemionkowicz, a Polish-born green card holder who has lived in the United States for decades, has spent nearly a year in ICE detention in Kentucky over old shoplifting convictions and allegations that she “forged documents to obtain immigration benefits,” a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Newsweek.

Siemionkowicz has been a green card holder since 2003 and has spent most of her adult life in the U.S. with her daughters, Claudia, 25, and Gabi, 21.

Donna Hughes-Brown, who was held at the same Kentucky detention facility as Siemionkowicz last year, told Newsweek that Siemionkowicz had already gone to court over the decades-old charges but “ICE had determined that it constitutes moral turpitude.” Under U.S. immigration law, certain offenses may be classified as crimes involving moral turpitude, a category that often includes crimes involving fraud, theft or dishonest conduct and can lead to deportation or other immigration penalties.

Read More on News

President Donald Trump has pledged to launch the largest mass deportation operation in U.S. history, and immigrants residing in the country both illegally and legally, with valid documentation such as green cards and visas, have been detained. Newsweek has reported dozens of cases involving green card holders and applicants who were swept up in the immigration raids and various arrests.

A DHS spokesperson added in an email to Newsweek, “Possessing a green card is a privilege, not a right. Under our nation’s laws, our government has the authority to revoke a green card if our laws are broken and abused.”

Newsweek has reached out to Siemionkowicz and her attorney for comment via email on Tuesday. Newsweek has reached out to her daughters via a GoFundMe for their mother’s legal fees and Claudia’s Instagram on Tuesday.

What To Know

Siemionkowicz was arrested on August 2, 2025, in Des Plaines, Illinois. She was gardening at her daughter Claudia’s home, The Chicago Tribune reported.

After two days at the Broadview facility outside of Chicago, she was transported to Campbell County Detention Center in Newport, Kentucky, where she has been held for nearly a year.

A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek that Siemionkowicz is a “criminal alien from Poland with multiple prior arrests for shoplifting.”

The statement continued, “She lawfully entered the United States on November 18, 1995. In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her lawful admission by failing to depart on or before February 16, 1996. She was granted a green card in January 2003.”

The DHS said she “forged documents to obtain immigration benefits” in 2001. DHS did not provide additional details when asked about the case.

The immigration agency noted that she had “been arrested twice in Illinois for retail theft: once in September 2005 and again in October 2011.”

In a GoFundMe started by her daughters, they note that “Beata and her family are aware of her two past minor theft charges, which she has owned up to,” adding that charges from 2001 and 2003 are of thefts that “equal less than $150.” Newsweek could not independently verify which 2001 and 2003 charges the daughters were referring to. The Tribune reported she has a misdemeanor retail theft from stores Jewel and Kohl’s in 2005 and 2011.

“For decades, Siemionkowicz has made a mockery of our immigration system and our laws,” the DHS spokesperson said, adding that “on December 9, 2025, an immigration judge issued Siemionkowicz an order of removal. She will remain in ICE custody pending her removal.”

Her family has filed an appeal and is working with Senator Dick Durbin to help get her out of detention. Newsweek has reached out to Durbin’s office for comment via email on Tuesday.

“Senator Durbin takes seriously his commitment to assist his constituents. Senator Durbin’s office has been in contact with the family and will continue to provide whatever assistance is possible,” a spokesperson from Durbin’s office told the Tribune.

Hughes-Brown told Newsweek that the DHS told Siemionkowicz there “were charges against her in Poland. But she has a letter from the Polish government stating there are no charges, nor have there ever been any charges against her in Poland.” Newsweek could not verify what charges the DHS was referring to.

CBS News reported that documents provided by the family included a February 2025 certification from the Polish Embassy stating that Siemionkowicz does not appear in Poland's national criminal registry.

Siemionkowicz has worked as a commercial cleaner and hospice caregiver in the Round Lake area, and her daughters note in the GoFundMe that she was the sole provider for the household. The Tribune reported that one of her daughters, Gabi, has temporarily dropped out of nursing school at Oakton College to help pay for her mother’s expenses, including her mortgage, utilities and legal fees.

“We just know deep down in our hearts that our mom does not deserve to be removed from this country,” Claudia told the Tribune, adding, “She has two misdemeanors, yes, but those were resolved. We’re really still in ignorance about the whole thing; we can’t believe that this is happening.”

The daughters started an Instagram page called Bring Beata Home to raise awareness of their mother's case. They captioned a July 3 video showing them meeting with various congressional leaders and advocating on their mother's behalf: "When it comes to our case, @dhsgov has failed to show ANY REAL PROOF as to why our mother has been in detention for the last 11 months."

Reported Conditions at Campbell County Detention Center

“We were there with women that were in for attempted murder charges. We were in with folks that had a lot of drug-related charges, a lot of domestic violence, a lot of hardcore criminal activities that basically ran the gamut, you name it,” Hughes-Brown told Newsweek about CCDC, where she and Siemionkowicz were held. The facility houses county, state, and federal inmates, according to its website.

Hughes-Brown, an Irish national and longtime green card holder, was released after 143 days in detention. DHS said she was detained because of two misdemeanors from 2015, which her husband said had been dealt with at the time. Under the Trump administration, such records have been reason to detain individuals at ports of entry, regardless of legal status.

“I had a bad check, an NSF [non-sufficient funds] charge in 2012 for $25 that was going through a grocery store,” she explained to Newsweek. She left the facility in December.

She said she was housed in an open dormitory-style unit with about 70 women, where only the shower and toilet area was separated by a wall. “There were feces in DS6 where Beata and I were first put. There was feces for some reason up above and blood and up above the doorway, the entryway,” she said.

Hughes-Brown continued, “Then the vents are covered like black mold all around all of the HVAC vents and the air return vents have black mold around them.” She noted that showers and toilets would be out of service for weeks at a time and women had very limited access to hygiene products and medical services.

Newsweek filled out a contact form for the CCDC for comment on Tuesday. Newsweek followed up with DHS and ICE for a comment on the matter.

In a previous comment related to a different story about conditions in ICE facilities, an ICE spokesperson told Newsweek on July 23, "It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody. This includes medical, dental, and mental health services as available, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. This is the best healthcare than many aliens have received in their entire lives."

Green Card Holders Detained

An estimated 12.8 million lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green card holders, live in the U.S. While green card holders have legal authorization to live and work in the country, they can still face detention and removal proceedings under certain circumstances, including some criminal convictions or alleged immigration violations.

Newsweek has reported on several recent cases involving green card holders detained by ICE, including Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia University graduate who was held for roughly three months before being released, Salah Sarsour, a Wisconsin imam who was detained over allegations related to his decades-old immigration paperwork and later released, and Dayton Andre Lindsay, a Jamaican citizen and longtime U.S. resident who remains in immigration custody while fighting removal proceedings, among others.

Federal data does not provide a public estimate of how many green card holders have been detained under Trump's second administration. However, immigration attorneys and advocacy groups have reported an increase in cases involving lawful permanent residents, particularly those with prior criminal convictions or alleged immigration violations. The DHS has argued that immigration enforcement actions are targeting individuals with criminal histories or immigration violations, stating “the worst of the worst” are being detained.

The Trump administration has deported more than 590,600 since January 2025, according to the administration's figures.

text:
PORTLAND – Immigration advocacy groups praised three new state laws coming onto the books this week aimed at restricting ICE activity in Maine.

The groups, including the ACLU of Maine, the Immigration Legal Advocacy Project and the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition, spoke to reporters Tuesday in advance of the new laws taking effect Wednesday.

“Together, these laws are proof that people in Maine and our elected officials will not sit idly by when our neighbors are in need,” said Zach Heiden, chief counsel for ACLU of Maine.

The three laws pertain to policing, rental property, and schools and state healthcare. More than a dozen other states nationwide have already passed similar legislation, the advocates said.

Regarding policing, ACLU of Maine Policy Director Michael Kebede said the laws in Maine will, among other protections:

Prohibit immigrants detained by ICE from being detained in Maine jails

Prohibit Maine jail officials from informing ICE of release dates for anyone being detained

Prohibit local police from handing prisoners over to ICE

Prohibit the use of ICE agents for interpretation services

Prohibit 287(g) agreements that would allow local law enforcement to work with ICE agents on immigration-related matters

“As rogue immigration agents become increasingly dangerous throughout the country and here in Maine, it’s more important than ever that our state and local officials have nothing to do with the chaos, fear, terror and lawlessness spread by ICE,” Kebede said.

Ben Gaines, legal director for Maine Equal Justice, said the laws also prevent landlords from disclosing information about their tenants to immigration officials. Gaines said he has heard reports that landlords have threatened to report tenants to ICE if they complain too much about their living conditions.

“We should all feel safe in the places where our families live, learn and heal,” he said.

The laws will also allow employees of public schools, state libraries and state healthcare facilities in Maine to deny ICE agents access to personal spaces or personal information without a warrant.

The advocates said the laws were passed prior to the shooting death of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by an ICE agent in Biddeford on July 13, but Ruben Torres, advocacy and policy director for the Maine Immigrant Rights’ Coalition, said the incident makes the new laws even more important.

“That moment reminded all of us that the decisions and the role the government plays in our lives are not abstract,” he said. “They affect our neighbors, our families and the trust that people place in the institutions that are meant to serve them.”

Sue Roche, executive director of the Immigration Legal Advocacy Project, noted that ICE agents are federal agents, but the new laws can still govern how Mainers interact with them.

“While Maine cannot completely bar ICE from our state because that agency is under federal jurisdiction, we can and we must maximize the tools and protections that we have available to us at the state and local level,” she said.

ICE and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Spectrum News.

text:
ICE agents deployed last summer to the Los Angeles area referred to the subjects of their immigration operations with racial slurs, according to newly released court documents.

On 4 July 2025, an unidentified agent wrote in a text chain, “btw tonks everywhere selling food for the 4th festivities in long beach right now,” invoking an anti-immigrant slur, which the US Border Patrol has previously warned against.

In a different string of messages sent on 2 July 2025, an agent wrote, “Some of these people are stupid. Why would you post on social media that you’re wet,” using the abbreviated version of a slur long used to denigrate undocumented Mexicans who crossed into America by the Rio Grande, a river stretching from Colorado into the Gulf of Mexico.

“Tonks” and “wet” also appeared in other correspondence.

The slurs were made public on Monday in a motion filed for a case five men brought against the Trump administration in June 2025, alleging that the stop and arrest practices of ICE agents during the Los Angeles raids were unlawful.

Lawyers for the men have requested that a federal judge bar any further detention stops based on race or socioeconomic status.

In June 2025, three of the men filing the lawsuit were arrested while waiting at a bus stop to be picked up for work. A fourth plaintiff had his arm twisted and was pushed against a gate during questioning by masked immigration agents, even as he explained he was a US citizen.

Maya Joachin, deputy director of immigrants’ rights at the ACLU foundation of Southern California, said in a press release the records evidenced “a pattern of racial profiling”.

She said: “Immigration officers are flagrantly violating the law by detaining people without justification and often primarily because of the color of their skin.”

Angel Santiago Tafolla, an Anaheim resident and US citizen who is not among the plaintiffs, said in a court declaration provided in the Monday filing that ICE agents swept through a car wash he worked at in Orange county.

He was handcuffed and put in a van before they realized he was an American citizen. “Other co-workers who are light-skinned also ran, but they were not chased. I feel that I was chased because I am a darker-skinned Latino,” Tafolla said.

In a December deposition, an ICE officer who led the bus stop operation suggested individuals loitering for work were flagged as possibly undocumented individuals. He described their appearance as “older Hispanic males”.

The raids were met with strong blowback from city and state officials. Tensions further flared, when Donald Trump sent the national guard to Los Angeles, citing a need to “liberate” the city from a “migrant invasion”, as protests erupted against ICE’s presence.

“Our agents are focused on protecting the American people – not entertaining performative outrage,” a spokesperson for the homeland security department said in a statement to CalMatters regarding the new court filings.

The DHS did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment.

text:
SAN ANTONIO, TX —On Tuesday, July 28, FWD.us and Families Belong Together held a press conference alongside U.S. Representative Joaquin Castro (TX-20) and members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus urging the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to release women, children and families locked away at the Dilley Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Detention Center.

Click here for a recording of the press conference.

The press conference was held shortly after the congressional delegation toured the South Texas family detention center, which has been wrought with reports of inhumane treatment. Congressman Castro was joined by Rep. Yassamin Ansari (AZ-3), Rep. Lizzie Fletcher (TX-7), Rep. Ayanna Pressley (MA-7), and Rep. Luz Rivas (CA-29). The members of Congress spoke on the troubling conditions they witnessed.
