text:
New conditions would require states to share voter data with the Department of Homeland Security

RICHMOND, Va. – Attorney General Jay Jones joined a coalition of 26 states to stop the Trump administration’s continued efforts to use federal funds—specifically, billions of dollars in federal counterterrorism and other emergency funds—to coerce states into complying with the administration’s political agenda. Part of this change requires states to transmit lists of all registered voters to The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and to assist DHS in enforcing federal immigration law.

“Critical funding for emergencies and counterterrorism efforts is not a bargaining chip, and Virginia will not be threatened or bullied into sharing sensitive voter data with the federal government,” said Attorney General Jones. “Donald Trump knows that the People will hold him accountable at the ballot box less than four months from now, so he is doing everything in his power to undermine voters before they get to the ballot box. With these funding conditions, he’s prioritizing his partisan agenda over the health and safety of those he serves. We will not let this stand.”

DHS and FEMA have established grant conditions for 2026 funding that again attempt to coerce the states into complying with the administration’s policy priorities. The conditions in total affect billions of dollars in funding, including over a billion dollars in Homeland Security Grant Program (HSGP) funding that states use to support security measures and protect residents from terrorism, cyberattacks and more. In 2023, more than $8.7 million were allocated through various federal grant programs to enhance emergency preparedness and security throughout the Commonwealth.

First, DHS and FEMA have again threatened to impose the same immigration conditions that they attempted to impose in 2025 on all federal grant programs. The conditions would require states to devote scarce law-enforcement resources to assist DHS in enforcing federal immigration law. These conditions were found to be unlawful and were enjoined by a district judge last year.

Second, DHS and FEMA threaten to withhold 20% of each state’s counterterrorism funding if states do not change state election law to conform to the administration’s policy goals. The attorneys general assert that these requirements would force states to abandon years of work and millions of dollars of investments in their elections systems, all to obtain unrelated funding that Congress earmarked for the prevention of terrorist attacks.

Specifically, the challenged funding conditions would require states to transition to paper-ballot systems, conduct a mandatory 5% manual audit of voting systems, reconcile voters and ballots using a methodology DHS has not disclosed, and use DHS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system to verify the citizenship of every election worker and every registered voter in state’s voter databases. If states do not comply, DHS and FEMA will withhold at least 20% of each state’s HSGP funding.

Finally, the challenged funding conditions unlawfully claim effectively unfettered power to terminate these grants on a whim. The agencies are attempting to add a condition that would allow FEMA to terminate any grant program for any reason. This constant threat of termination undermines the stability and reliability that these critical programs rely on to be effective.

The attorney’s general argue in this lawsuit that the grant conditions violate the Administrative Procedure Act and the U.S. Constitution’s Spending Clause.

Joining Attorney General Jones in filing the lawsuit are attorneys general of California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin, as well as the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.

title: Suit alleges DHS targeted people observing and protesting immigration agents
description:
“In response, DHS decided to record the Americans who were peacefully observing its agents,” the suit says.
In Minnesota, legal observers tailing DHS agents in a car would commonly be led back to their own home addresses, according to the suit.
Chilling rights The suit alleges DHS’ actions have had a chilling effect on First Amendment-protected activity.
A Global Entry ombudsman provides “additional oversight” of some cases, the spokesperson said.
A denial of Global Entry is not an impediment to travel, they wrote.
text:
Three people who observed federal immigration enforcement during the Trump administration’s sometimes-violent surge said in a federal lawsuit filed Friday that the Homeland Security Department illegally recorded them and revoked their status in the department’s trusted traveler programs.

The suit, filed in the Southern District of California, says the administration violated a federal privacy law, administrative law and the First Amendment by targeting people who observed and protested aggressive immigration enforcement, including during the deadly operation in Minneapolis in January.

The Electronic Privacy Information Center, a legal group that advocates for privacy issues related to technology, is also a plaintiff in the case.

Amid a nationwide surge of immigration enforcement that has included federal agents shooting and killing protesters, observers and immigrants, opponents “did what anyone is supposed to do when they disagree with government action: They exercised their First Amendment rights” by assembling, protesting and recording DHS agents’ activity in public, the suit says.

“In response, DHS decided to record the Americans who were peacefully observing its agents,” the suit says.

Officers with the DHS agencies Immigration and Customs Protection and Border Patrol killed two observers, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis in incidents 17 days apart in January.

"Driven home by ICE"

ICE and Border Patrol agents used facial recognition technology, license plate readers and other technology to identify protesters and observers. The agents would then use that information in efforts to intimidate and retaliate against protesters, the suit says.

Federal immigration officers addressed many legal observers by name, despite having never spoken to them. In Minnesota, legal observers tailing DHS agents in a car would commonly be led back to their own home addresses, according to the suit.

“The experience … is so widespread that Minnesota residents have coined a term for it: being ‘driven home by ICE,’” the suit said.

The practice shows that DHS is no longer following its own 2023 policy on facial recognition, the suit says. The department quietly removed the policy from its website — omitting it even from a set of archived pages — during President Donald Trump’s first month back in office, the suit says.

The complaint argues that amounted to a policy change, which DHS did not conduct through the process agencies must follow under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The department also retaliated against protesters and observers by revoking their status in DHS trusted traveler programs TSA Precheck and Global Entry, the suit says.

Nicole Cleland, a Minnesota woman who is one of the individual plaintiffs in the suit, said Global Entry status was revoked three days after an encounter with a Border Patrol agent whom she was following at a safe distance, according to the suit.

Chilling rights

The suit alleges DHS’ actions have had a chilling effect on First Amendment-protected activity.

Cleland has stopped observing DHS operations for fear of further retaliation, according to the suit.

The two other individuals who brought the suit, Jacquelyn Ivey of South Carolina and Anna Walker of California, said they experienced “fear, anxiety and emotional distress” following their interactions with DHS officers.

The suit also mentions activity in Maine, North Carolina and Chicago.

DHS response

In response to a request to DHS for comment, a spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection, which administers Global Entry, said trusted traveler status can be denied for “inability to demonstrate low-risk traveler status.”

“Global Entry or other CBP Trusted Traveler Program memberships are not revoked because someone exercises their First Amendment rights,” the spokesperson wrote. “Membership may be denied or revoked for reasons such as criminal activity (including pending charges or warrants), violations of customs or immigration laws, or inability to demonstrate low-risk traveler status.”

The spokesperson added that travelers whose Global Entry is denied or revoked can ask for additional review. A Global Entry ombudsman provides “additional oversight” of some cases, the spokesperson said.

A denial of Global Entry is not an impediment to travel, they wrote.

DHS did not respond to questions about its policies for recording or using facial recognition on observers.

description:

text:
A Mississippi taxi driver accused of exploiting and coercing immigrants released from an Adams County prison has operated the scheme for far longer than previously known—and, according to new information obtained by The Mississippi Independent, is among dozens of drivers profiting from a broader predatory taxi market in the state and in neighboring Louisiana.

Karen Hester, a longtime immigration activist who helps facilitate the release and transportation of immigrants from detention centers across the United States, said via email that she had used Otis Anderson’s Natchez-based taxi service for years to transport immigrants to airports in Mississippi and Louisiana.

“I have over the course of perhaps the last 5-6 years paid $325 plus for maybe 5-6 asylum seekers leaving Adams with Anderson taxi,” she told The Mississippi Independent, referring to the Adams County Correctional Center just outside Natchez, Mississippi. “I’ve always thought it was a racket as ICE should be transporting them,” she added, citing the agency’s gargantuan funding.

It turns out Anderson’s operation is not an isolated case.

Interviews with immigration advocates and lawyers, along with fare quotes obtained from Louisiana and Mississippi taxi companies listed in ICE documents, reveal that Anderson’s business is part of a broader system of apparently independent drivers who charge immigrants between $300 and $1,150 per person to reach airports and other transportation hubs after their release from detention.

Immigration advocates say the exploitative market has taken root amid ICE’s years-long failure to enforce federal detention standards requiring ICE officials and staff at privately operated facilities to transport detainees to local transportation hubs during operating hours. Instead, immigrants are routinely released from remote facilities with few practical ways to leave, creating a captive market for drivers able to demand exorbitant fares from people with little money, limited English and no knowledge of the area. Sometimes the drivers have well-connected spouses or partners on the inside.

Meanwhile, nonprofit organizations offering free transportation have been sidelined, advocacy groups say.

“We have always cared a lot about the taxi situation,” said Frances Kelley, Shreveport coordinator for the Louisiana Advocates for Immigrants in Detention, or LA-AID. “Because it was what was right in front of us, and what we were seeing, and we were hearing about people having to pay these exorbitant amounts of money.”

Kelley added: “There’s some kind of arrangement because the taxi drivers would get called and we wouldn’t.”

Rulebreakers

As The Mississippi Independent reported last month, Anderson was accused of threatening to have a recently released immigrant child returned to detention at the Adams County facility if he could not find a way to pay the $300 taxi fare to Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport. The child, Aurelio Cornejo Serrano, said two other immigrants were also charged $300 each for the same trip.

His uncle paid the fare, according to text messages between the uncle and Anderson that were shared with The Mississippi Independent and the Spanish-language newspaper El Molino Informativo. The cellphone number in the messages was confirmed as Anderson’s after he responded to texts from The Mississippi Independent.

What distinguishes Anderson from other drivers charging rates as much as three times a standard Uber fare is that his wife is employed by CoreCivic, the private company that operates the Adams County detention facility. Tameka Moore-Anderson works on the receiving and discharge team. One of the unit’s responsibilities is arranging and approving transportation for immigrants being released.

CoreCivic, like all private companies and government agencies operating immigration detention facilities, is legally required to follow a series of federal rules when preparing detainees for release. Those rules include allowing a detainee one free telephone call to “facilitate release arrangements,” according to the latest National Detention Standards, updated in June 2026. The standards also say that “when appropriate,” detainees are to be taken by facility staff to a transportation station while it is still open.

The exception applies when a public transportation hub is within one mile of the facility, in which case detainees are to be given an information sheet with directions and available transportation options, according to the standards. The Adams County detention facility, like almost every immigration detention center in Mississippi and Louisiana, is not located within one mile of public transportation, meaning transportation should be provided by the facility, per federal rules. The nearest town with transportation options is Natchez, 12 miles away.

Yet transportation is rarely provided and is unlikely to be in the future, advocacy groups say.

“If they’re not going to fix the things where people’s lives are at risk, they’re not going to fix this,” Kelley said, referring to a slew of other complaints made against ICE facilities, including disgusting, barbaric, negligent, abusive and unsafe conditions.

For years, nonprofit organizations and volunteers collaborated with staff at detention facilities to transport large groups of released detainees. LA-AID regularly collected people from facilities in Louisiana and from Adams County. The organization operated out of an abandoned church where immigrants could shower, eat, find clothing and receive advice. Those without money could sometimes receive help paying for a plane or bus ticket.

But after the White House ended discretionary releases in early 2025, the need for such a large transport operation dried up.

“They told me that they were not allowed to release people anymore,” Kelley said. “And then they obviously stopped asking me to receive people.”

For years, immigrant advocacy groups have argued that detention centers in Louisiana and Mississippi have failed to meet the Performance-Based National Detention Standards, even as government audits declared the facilities compliant.

LA-AID filed a civil rights complaint with the Office of Inspector General in 2021 regarding what it described as “blatant” violations at facilities across Louisiana and Mississippi. The complaint focused in particular on failures to allow detainees to contact family members and instances in which people were left waiting in detention-center lobbies or outside overnight without being able to contact anyone.

A response from the OIG said the agency had shared the letter with internal departments “for their consideration as they plan future oversight activities.”

Why free transportation disappeared

How the situation reached this point is wrapped up in a series of complex and overlapping legal interpretations.

Federal policy changes in 2025 sharply curtailed ICE’s use of discretionary release and barred immigration judges from granting bond to immigrants who entered the country without inspection, regardless of how long they had lived in the U.S. The Fifth Circuit, which governs federal courts in Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas, upheld that interpretation, although four other appellate courts rejected it and some warned that it raised serious due-process concerns. Immigrants in detention began to swell to record numbers, by design: In January 2025, the Trump administration established quotas to increase the number of arrests from a few hundred per day to at least 1,200 to 1,500, increasing the chances that non-criminals would be detained; the following June, that number was increased to 3,000 per day.

With no bond remedy available and a shortage of immigration judges under the Trump administration, detainees filed more than 63,000 habeas petitions in federal court, asking judges to determine whether their detention was lawful and, in some cases, to order a bond hearing or release. Nearly 650 such cases have been filed in Mississippi’s Southern District, though the court has not granted relief to any detainee or issued substantive decisions in more than a handful of cases.

Declining releases has meant far less demand for nonprofit organizations and volunteers to transport released detainees. Yet some people who do not fall under those rulings are still being released, which should, in theory, make it easier for ICE and the private companies operating the detention centers to provide transportation or contact nonprofit organizations to help.

Taxi list doesn’t add up

Instead, detainees awaiting release are given a list of suggested local taxi options. The ICE-approved list serves seven of Louisiana’s nine detention facilities and the Adams County facility in Mississippi.

The Mississippi Independent obtained a November 2022 version of the list from an attorney representing an immigrant released from the Adams County facility in October 2025. Of the 23 taxi companies on the 2022 list contacted by The Mississippi Independent, two were no longer operating as taxi services, two telephone numbers were disconnected, two companies said the trip was too far, one number belonged to a limousine driver and another connected to the main office of Monroe, Louisiana’s public bus service. The two numbers listed for local Adams County taxi services, which would presumably be the most convenient and least expensive, were either disconnected or did not belong to a taxi service.

Ten taxi services did not respond. Four reported offering quotes ranging from $300 to $1,150. The quotes included some combination of a taxi ride, hotel stay and flights from Baton Rouge to New York City, a destination selected at random. One driver quoted $650 for the taxi ride alone. All four responding drivers were based in Monroe or Alexandria, Louisiana, both about two hours from Adams County.

The detainee released in October 2025 was ultimately transported by Anderson, even though his taxi service does not appear on the 2022 ICE taxi list provided to the detainee’s attorney. The Mississippi Independent obtained a separate ICE taxi list, from November 2025, from LA-AID. Anderson’s taxi service was also absent from that list. What is odd about the omissions is that James Wynn, another Natchez taxi driver, told The Mississippi Independent that he had seen Anderson at the detention facility repeatedly over several years, loading groups of newly released immigrants into a passenger van.

An individual detainee, relative or attorney could have found Anderson’s services online, but it is hard to explain how groups of detainees—independently detained, with limited access to phones and internet—would all somehow locate the same unlisted driver and coordinate a shared pickup. Their relatives and attorneys, when they had them, would have been scattered across the country and generally would have had no way to coordinate with one another. These circumstances raise a fundamental question: Who was arranging for Anderson to collect large groups of detainees simultaneously?

The Mississippi Independent also found a 15-passenger van advertised for sale by Anderson on an Adams County Facebook listing page, alongside a smaller minivan, suggesting that his business was equipped to transport larger groups. The larger van had “Anderson Transportation Natchez” printed on the door. The Mississippi Independent asked Anderson and CoreCivic whether Anderson’s wife, a senior officer in the receiving and discharge unit, or any other employee at the facility, had referred released detainees to his service or arranged the group pickups. Anderson did not respond. CoreCivic said only that its employees provide released immigrants with information about local transportation but do not select or contract with private drivers.

“When our government partners direct that an individual is to be released directly from our facility, our staff provide these individuals with information regarding local transportation options to help them reach their preferred destination,” CoreCivc said in an emailed statement. “CoreCivic does not have any contracts with private transportation companies for this purpose, nor do we receive any financial benefit from such companies. Individuals are free to make their own transportation arrangements, including those arranged by their legal representatives.”

The company also pointed to its Human Rights Policy, which outlines its commitments regarding the rights and treatment of people held in its facilities.

Moore-Anderson did not respond to questions about whether she helps provide transportation information to detainees, whether she or discharge staff recommend Anderson’s service or whether she had disclosed her relationship with him to CoreCivic. The company did not answer questions about the safeguards it uses to identify potential conflicts of interest among employees involved in releases.

Complaints do not prompt changes

Hester said she and fellow immigration activist Pat Leach had complained about transportation practices at detention facilities in the past but saw little change.

“I am sure we all know we are being scammed but have no choice as the power is with Adams—the internment camps,” Leach said in an email to The Mississippi Independent.

Leach said he had encountered similar “extortion” practices in California, suggesting the problem extends beyond Louisiana and Mississippi. At the Imperial Regional Detention Facility in Calexico, he said, drivers charged what he described as very expensive fares to people with few other options.

In another case, Leach said, a woman released at night from an ICE detention facility in California City refused to leave because no transportation was available.

“It is in the middle of nowhere,” he said. “She refused to leave the detention until mid-morning next day when her lawyer paid for an Uber to Los Angeles to her office.”

Questions remain about how transportation options are selected at Adams County, why advocates stopped receiving advance notice of releases and whether CoreCivic has adequately addressed the potential conflict created by a discharge officer’s husband repeatedly transporting people from the facility for hundreds of dollars per passenger.

For immigrants leaving detention, the opening of the facility doors may mark the end of their incarceration. But in remote parts of Louisiana and Mississippi, it does not necessarily mean they are free to leave.

text:
With this rule, USCIS can refer asylum applications to Immigration Judges without interviewing the alien

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) announced a rule change designed to reduce the backlog in the asylum system.

Currently, both USCIS and Department of Justice (DOJ) Immigration Judges adjudicate applications for asylum: USCIS adjudicates “affirmative” asylum applications for aliens who are not in removal proceedings, while Immigration Judges adjudicate “defensive” asylum applications for aliens who are in removal proceedings. Depending on the alien’s immigration status, USCIS will usually either adjudicate the application or refer it to an Immigration Judge, who will then conduct a new review of the application. This essentially allows an alien to get a second chance at asylum.

The interim final rule allows USCIS to refer asylum applications to Immigration Judges without first interviewing the alien. This rule will shorten the total time that it takes asylum officers and Immigration Judges to adjudicate asylum applications. Among other reasons, USCIS is making this change to reduce the asylum backlog.

“For far too long the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection,” said USCIS Director Joseph Edlow. “America’s asylum system exists to protect individuals who genuinely fear persecution and this rule will help ensure that resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole.”

“One of the greatest barriers to effective immigration enforcement is intentional delay by illegal aliens and the open borders attorneys who represent them,” said DHS General Counsel James Percival. “My office works every day with the immigration components of DHS to improve efficiency and fulfill the President’s mandate. The rule would do just that.”

The new rule will go into effect immediately. USCIS will accept public comments and later issue a final rule responding to those comments.

Dive Brief:

More students could begin the new school year without consistent access to food and healthcare in the wake of a new immigration-related federal rule, a leading K-12 group warns.

The final rule, issued July 20 by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, will cause a “chilling effect” by allowing immigration officials to deny applications for permanent residency or visa extensions to noncitizens who use school meals and other public benefits like Medicaid or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, said AASA, The School Superintendents Association, in a Wednesday blog post.

DHS projected $13 billion in savings to the federal and state governments once noncitizens are disenrolled from these programs. AASA, meanwhile, said those savings could at least partially fall on schools, which frequently act as a “primary safety net” when students lose access to key healthcare and nutrition services.

Dive Insight:

If fewer students participate in benefits programs like SNAP and Medicaid, schools will feel a trickle-down effect, AASA warned. That’s because those programs’ rolls are used to help schools qualify for direct certification under the Community Eligibility Provision — whereby all students are eligible for free school meals and families don’t have to apply separately — and for access to School-Based Medicaid services.

A school or district qualifies for CEP if at least 25% of its students are eligible for free or reduced-price school meals. Direct certification automatically identifies students eligible for free or reduced-price school meals if they are already enrolled in a means-tested federal program like SNAP or Medicaid.

In the 2025-26 school year, a record number of schools — 55,362 — offered free breakfast and lunch to all of their students through CEP, according to a new report by the Food Research and Action Center. While school participation increased by 2.1%, FRAC said the “pace of growth slowed substantially” in comparison to previous years.

In total, 27.6 million children attended a CEP school in 2025-26, FRAC found. Three-quarters of eligible schools adopted CEP last school year.

Concerns over the impact on students and schools from the new DHS rule come in the wake of earlier warnings from policy advocates that cuts to these programs in the past year would hurt families.

Both FRAC and the Center for American Progress have flagged that access to free meals through CEP could be jeopardized by the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s significant cuts to SNAP and Medicaid.

Since the 1-year-old law took effect in July 2025, FRAC estimates that over 5 million people have already lost their SNAP benefits.

DHS said it received 8,846 public comments on its new rule, a majority of which expressed opposition.

Some commenters shared concerns that parents would withdraw their children from early childhood education programs like Head Start for fear of risking their immigration status, DHS noted. A resulting enrollment decline could in turn destabilize funding for Head Start and accelerate closures of centers. Other commenters also pointed out that immigrant families could disenroll in SNAP, which would harm their children’s access to food and could ultimately hurt a child’s ability to participate in school.

In response, DHS acknowledged in its final rule that many federal benefit programs aim to improve economic and future outcomes for children and their families and that families might decide to disenroll their child to “avoid negative immigration consequences.”

DHS added, however, that the rule “restores broad discretion to evaluate all pertinent facts and aligns with long-standing policy that aliens in the United States should be self-reliant and government benefits should not incentivize immigration.”

A federal law that prohibits states from granting immigrants unlawfully in the country secondary education tuition breaks unless they give those same benefits to all US citizens regardless of residency expressly preempts the provisions, Judge David W. Dugan of the US District Court for the Southern District of Illinois said July 24.

The federal law “is an exercise of the federal government’s exclusive authority ‘over the subject of immigration and the status of aliens,’” Dugan wrote. It doesn’t run afoul of the anti-commandeering doctrine because it doesn’t dictate what a state may or may not do education-wise; it acts solely to limit private individuals’ eligibility for certain benefits, Dugan said.

“Put simply, U.S. citizens or nationals must be treated no worse than illegal aliens,” Dugan said.

The state provisions provide eligibility for in-state tuition benefits to such immigrants so long as they resided in the state or proved they resided there at one time, such a graduation from an Illinois high school.

The US Justice Department has sued several state over their in-state tuition programs for unlawful immigrants and struck immediate settlements with several red states, includingTexas, Oklahoma, and Nebraska.

“Illinois sought to incentivize illegal immigration on the taxpayer’s dime by treating illegal aliens better than U.S. citizens living in other states, in clear violation of federal law,” said U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft in a press release. “This ruling enforces the statute Congress wrote and stops the State from putting illegal aliens ahead of American citizens.”

The Illinois Attorney General’s Office is reviewing the decision and evaluating its options, said April McLaren, deputy press secretary for Attorney General Kwame Raoul (D).

description:
More than 300,000 Haitian immigrants are set to lose their ability to legally live and work in the U.S. on Monday, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is reportedly preparing to escalate its operations to arrest and deport some of them.
Ohio will reportedly be heavily targeted, particularly Springfield, where President Donald Trump had, in 2024, falsely accused Haitian migrants of eating residents’ pets.
A potential crackdown on Haitian migrants follows the Supreme Court’s June ruling that allowed the Trump Administration, for the time being, to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation for those fleeing violence and natural disaster in Haiti and Syria.
In February, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Administration’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation, though the Trump Administration appealed, eventually leading to the Supreme Court ruling.
‘A huge mistake’ Some Republicans have opposed the Trump Administration’s plan to end the TPS designation for Haiti.
text:
More than 300,000 Haitian immigrants are set to lose their ability to legally live and work in the U.S. on Monday, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is reportedly preparing to escalate its operations to arrest and deport some of them.

Those expanded operations could start as early as this week, according to reports from Fox News and CBS News, which cite unnamed federal sources. Ohio will reportedly be heavily targeted, particularly Springfield, where President Donald Trump had, in 2024, falsely accused Haitian migrants of eating residents’ pets.

A potential crackdown on Haitian migrants follows the Supreme Court’s June ruling that allowed the Trump Administration, for the time being, to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation for those fleeing violence and natural disaster in Haiti and Syria. The binding mandate of that ruling is expected to be transmitted to lower courts on Monday.

It remains unclear how aggressive the reported ICE campaign will be, and if Haiti can successfully reintegrate an influx of returnees. But Jean Négot Bonheur Delva, director-general of Haiti’s National Office of Migration, told local media earlier this month that following a conversation with the U.S. embassy in the country, Haitians should expect weekly deportation flights carrying about 250 former TPS status grantees.

The court ruling and its expected implementation have stirred anxiety among Haitians in the U.S. who could lose their livelihoods and may be sent back to the crisis-stricken Caribbean nation. It could also have a profound impact on the U.S. economy. A January 2026 fact sheet from immigration advocacy group FWD.us estimates that about 200,000 Haitian TPS holders are in the U.S. workforce, including 15,000 agricultural workers, 13,000 nursing assistants, and thousands of others in various industries.

In a statement to CBS News, DHS said it “does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” adding: “What we would say now is it’s closing time which means you don't have to go home, but you can't stay here… The good news is it's not too late to get a $2,600 check and a free flight home.”

Conditions in Haiti still severe

During his first-term Administration, Trump targeted TPS, a program since 1990 that has allowed migrants from designated countries with unsafe conditions—such as armed conflict, natural disaster, epidemics, or other extraordinary conditions—to reside and work legally in the U.S.

In his second-term Administration, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved to terminate TPS designations for several countries, including Ethiopia, Myanmar, and Yemen. In many announcements ending those protections, then-Secretary Kristi Noem emphasized that TPS was designed to be temporary, and she argued that the living conditions in many of the countries with TPS designation have improved. Any extension to the TPS designations for those countries, the department said, would be “contrary” to the “national interest.”

Persons who lose their TPS status must find another lawful basis for staying in the U.S. or depart the U.S.; otherwise they may be removed.

But these TPS rescissions and terminations have been legally challenged. In February, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Administration’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation, though the Trump Administration appealed, eventually leading to the Supreme Court ruling.

Haiti first received a TPS designation in 2010 after a magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck the country in January that year, leaving more than 300,000 people dead and displacing over a million others. Since then, the country has been a TPS designee: the first-term Trump Administration’s planned termination was delayed mainly due to court injunctions and other rulings, and the succeeding Biden Administration renewed and extended those designations.

As DHS Secretary, Noem reviewed Haiti’s TPS designation and her department found that there were no “extraordinary and temporary conditions” that prevented Haitian nationals from returning safely, and that even if there were, allowing them to stay longer in the U.S. went against national interest.

The State Department, however, notes that conditions in the country are not that safe: as of July 10, it holds the highest-level travel warning to Americans, urging them not to visit. A state of national emergency has been in effect since 2024 because of gang-linked criminality and violence: an estimated 26 gangs, at times heavily armed, control 90% of the capital Port-au-Prince and its surrounding areas, and the nation’s government has had a hard time putting the situation under control.

According to the latest report by the International Organization for Migration, the violence in Haiti has displaced nearly 1.5 million persons, of whom more than half are women and girls.

‘A huge mistake’

Some Republicans have opposed the Trump Administration’s plan to end the TPS designation for Haiti.

In April, the GOP-controlled House passed legislation that would require the Homeland Security Secretary to redesignate Haiti to TPS until a few months into 2029, with 10 Republicans siding with Democrats. The legislation is now pending in the Senate, where the latest attempt to pass it was blocked on July 22 by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R, Mo.). But even if the bill passes both chambers, the White House earlier said that the President’s advisers would recommend vetoing it.

Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R, Fla.) told CBS News earlier this month that while Haiti is a “failed state,” he thinks “deporting Haitians that are under TPS right now, back to Haiti, would be a huge mistake.”

Markwayne Mullin, who took over for Noem as DHS Secretary in March, defended the decision to end Haiti’s TPS designation. Speaking to CNN in June, Mullin said that those staying in the U.S. under TPS have “had plenty of time” to explore other options to legally stay in the U.S. long-term, instead of banking solely on what was intended to be a temporary measure.

Asked about whether Haiti qualified as “safe,” Mullin told CNN that such a qualification “isn’t quite just that simple,” and he argued that the State Department travel advisory had Americans in mind and not Haitians.

text:
On Friday 24 July 2026, from 8.00-9.00am, activists converged on Aviva’s historic Norwich headquarters. They were demanding the insurer severs ties with companies accused of human rights abuses against migrants and asylum seekers.

They brought a 1.5m barbed wire ball surrounding Aviva’s logo, and spoke to hundreds of staff as they made their way to work.

Aviva insures the largest number of migrant detention and surveillance contractors operating in the UK. Activists say this record sits in stark contradiction to the company’s publicly stated human rights commitments.

Profiting from abuse?

Aviva, which grew out of Norwich Union to become a multinational company, positions itself as a leader on corporate human rights. Yet campaigners allege the insurer is failing to uphold its own due diligence policies.

They point out it continues to underwrite private corporations accused of serious human rights violations connected to the detention and surveillance of migrants and asylum seekers. These companies include Serco and Mears.

Activists are specifically calling on Aviva to drop its insurance contract with Serco, which comes up for renewal on 31 October 2026. Campaigner for Boycott Bloody Insurance, Andrew Taylor said:

Aviva’s five-plus years of cover have enabled Serco’s continued operation of immigration detention centres, round-the-clock surveillance of migrants, and substandard housing provision. Aviva has continued to insure Serco after reports of sexual abuse, human rights abuses and fraud. It’s time for Aviva to break ties with Serco.

Local context: migrant housing in Norwich

The action carries particular weight in Norwich. In 2025, the city saw a surge of anti-migrant protests outside hotels housing asylum seekers. Occupants and staff faced harassment and assault.

Following the closure of the Brook Hotel in Bowthorpe, there are currently no hotels in Norfolk housing asylum seekers, according to Home Office data. But campaigners say the underlying detention system remains intact.

Representing Nelson Ward in Norwich, Green Party councillor Hannah Hoechner said:

Serco’s role in the UK’s immigration system is a stark reminder of what happens when government outsources responsibility for vulnerable people’s lives.

Despite serious concerns raised about the treatment of those detained in Serco-run facilities, the company continues to be awarded contracts worth billions from the UK government.

The UK’s asylum system should be built on dignity, compassion and accountability—not on contracts that allow private companies to put profit over basic human rights.

What activists are demanding:

Aviva drops its insurance contract with Serco before its renewal on 31 October 2026.

Aviva conducts transparent, independently verifiable human rights due diligence on all clients involved in migrant detention and surveillance.

Aviva publicly reports on the steps taken to align its underwriting portfolio with its human rights commitments.

text:
OAKLAND, Calif. — The American Civil Liberties Union of Northern California is accusing the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office of denying its own documented history of racial misconduct after the office disputed allegations in a court filing that a former prosecutor held racist views, despite disciplinary records showing he used a racial slur during court proceedings in the 1990s.

According to the ACLU of Northern California, the dispute centers on a legal response filed by the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office in the case of Darren Stanley.

The organization contends the filing denied allegations that former Deputy District Attorney Theodore “Ted” Landswick held racist views or used a racial slur during judicial proceedings, despite disciplinary records from 1994 documenting the incident.

The ACLU argues the office’s current position conflicts with its own documented history, pointing to a 1994 disciplinary letter issued by then-Alameda County District Attorney John Meehan.

According to the ACLU, the letter states that Landswick repeatedly used a racial slur while referring to two Black individuals during court proceedings.

Following the misconduct, Meehan reportedly reassigned Landswick from felony trial duties and reduced his salary, describing his conduct as “offensive and degrading.”

The ACLU argues the incident is part of a broader pattern of historical prosecutorial misconduct within the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office that continues to affect confidence in the criminal legal system.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, a federal judge in 2024 found “strong evidence” of a pattern of prosecutorial misconduct involving jury selection in multiple Alameda County death penalty cases.

That ruling prompted a review of dozens of capital cases after prosecutors’ notes were found to contain derogatory comments about prospective Black and Jewish jurors.

Additional litigation has since sought to examine those historical practices and their impact on past convictions.

According to The Associated Press, two men whose convictions were overturned because of prosecutorial misconduct sued Alameda County in June 2026, alleging prosecutors systematically excluded Black and Jewish jurors from death penalty trials during the 1990s.

The lawsuits allege the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office knew about discriminatory jury selection practices that deprived defendants of fair trials.

Although those allegations remain the subject of civil litigation, Alameda County has not admitted wrongdoing. The ACLU argues that acknowledging documented misconduct is necessary to ensure accountability and restore public trust.

The organization has urged the District Attorney’s Office to review cases that may have been affected by discriminatory practices and to consider the office’s documented history when responding to claims before the courts.

As of publication, the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office had not publicly responded to the ACLU’s July 23 statement.

According to the office’s website, District Attorney Ursula Jones Dickson has continued issuing news releases announcing criminal prosecutions and other office initiatives.

The office also has not publicly addressed the ACLU’s allegations concerning historical prosecutorial misconduct.

The ACLU maintains that the dispute extends beyond a single court filing and raises broader questions about how prosecutors confront documented misconduct from prior administrations.

The Alameda County District Attorney’s Office, however, has challenged the specific allegations presented in the Stanley litigation.

As the case moves forward, the courts will determine the legal merits of those competing claims, while the broader debate over accountability for historical prosecutorial misconduct continues.

title: DHS accused of tracking immigration observers and retaliating through Global Entry
description:
Nicole Cleland, a Minnesota resident, was observing vehicles she believed carried federal immigration agents on January 10 when a Border Patrol agent approached her car, according to the complaint.
Three days later, DHS revoked her Global Entry and TSA PreCheck without explanation.
Jacquelyn Ivey of South Carolina went to Charlotte, North Carolina, in November 2025 to observe an immigration enforcement surge.
The lawsuit identifies DHS’s Automated Targeting System (ATS) as one possible link between street-level encounters and decisions affecting Global Entry.
They also seek to bar the government from using such information to deny Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or other benefits.
text:
A federal lawsuit accuses the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of collecting the faces, license plates, and identities of people peacefully observing immigration enforcement, then using those records to revoke Global Entry and Transportation Security Administration (TSA) PreCheck privileges.

The 55-page complaint, filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, was brought by the Electronic Privacy Information Center and three U.S. citizens who say federal agents photographed, scanned, or identified them while they observed immigration operations.

Each lost Trusted Traveler status soon afterward.

The plaintiffs allege DHS adopted an undisclosed policy allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) personnel to create and retain records on people protesting or recording federal operations, even when they had committed no crime.

The lawsuit infers the policy from repeated conduct in several states, internal instructions to collect information on protesters, the removal of privacy safeguards, and DHS’s acknowledgment that information gathered during encounters with people who are not arrested can become an official government record.

It does not establish which systems contain the plaintiffs’ information.

The allegations have not been tested in court. CBP denied that Trusted Traveler memberships are revoked in retaliation for protected speech, saying status may be withdrawn for criminal activity, outstanding warrants, customs or immigration violations, or an inability to demonstrate that a person remains a low-risk traveler.

Nicole Cleland, a Minnesota resident, was observing vehicles she believed carried federal immigration agents on January 10 when a Border Patrol agent approached her car, according to the complaint.

The agent called Cleland by name although she had not identified herself, told her he had facial recognition and that his body camera was operating, then accused her of impeding federal operations. Three days later, DHS revoked her Global Entry and TSA PreCheck without explanation.

Cleland alleges she had no other recent law enforcement contact. Her status had not been restored when the lawsuit was filed, and she says the encounter caused her to stop observing immigration operations because she feared arrest.

Jacquelyn Ivey of South Carolina went to Charlotte, North Carolina, in November 2025 to observe an immigration enforcement surge. As she recorded suspected federal agents, several armed agents surrounded her car. One pointed a phone at her face, photographed her license plate, and demanded her driver’s license, telling her she could not leave until she was identified.

Her Global Entry was revoked ten days later. DHS eventually reinstated it but never explained the decision or confirmed that records created during the encounter had been deleted, the complaint says.

Anna Walker of San Diego followed a suspected federal vehicle through a public Target parking lot on April 1. Two other vehicles boxed in her car while agents aimed phones at her face and photographed her license plate. She was allowed to leave after calling 911.

Walker discovered five days later that her Global Entry had been revoked. After a reporter questioned DHS, her membership was restored, but she received no assurance that the underlying information had been erased.

The case turns partly on what DHS means when it denies maintaining a database of protesters.

In an April response to lawmakers, then-acting ICE Director Todd Lyons denied that ICE operated a database of U.S. citizens protesting its activities or a separate system for people encountered but not arrested.

Lyons nevertheless acknowledged that agents may collect biographic, biometric, and situational information when they believe someone may be interfering with operations or creating a safety concern.

Lyons also said information recorded during an encounter with someone who is neither arrested nor detained becomes an official government record and may be supplemented with open source material and records from other law enforcement agencies.

Biometric Update reported last week that ICE has established an extensive covert social media monitoring capability.

The plaintiffs do not claim DHS created a system formally labeled as a protester database. They argue that the Privacy Act applies whenever an agency collects or maintains an identifiable record, including a photograph, biometric image, or license plate retrievable by a person’s name or another identifier.

The lawsuit cites a January memorandum circulated among agents deployed to Minnesota directing them to capture images, license plates, identification, and information about protesters and alleged agitators in a consolidated form.

It also recounts reports of agents scanning observers’ faces with the Mobile Fortify application and addressing people by name without any visible prior interaction.

In Maine, legal observers alleged agents photographed their faces and vehicles while threatening to place them on a domestic terrorism watchlist. DHS has denied maintaining such a database.

The lawsuit identifies DHS’s Automated Targeting System (ATS) as one possible link between street-level encounters and decisions affecting Global Entry.

ATS can search law enforcement and intelligence holdings, use commercial information such as license plate records, and assemble a consolidated view of data associated with a person.

Its facial recognition functions allow agents to upload a photograph and search DHS holdings for a possible match.

ATS is CBP’s principal vetting tool for Trusted Traveler programs. Global Entry members are continuously vetted, allowing CBP to reconsider their status when new derogatory information becomes available.

The complaint does not prove that information on Cleland, Ivey, and Walker was entered into ATS. It alleges that records on observers are maintained in or accessible through ATS or another DHS system, and that the timing of the revocations supports an inference that information collected during the encounters was used.

The plaintiffs contend ATS’s public notice authorizes its use for border security, customs, immigration enforcement, and counterterrorism, but not for maintaining records on people merely because they observed or protested immigration operations.

The lawsuit also challenges the Trump administration’s removal of two safeguards in early 2025.

A 2023 directive prohibited DHS from using facial recognition or face capture to target someone solely for exercising constitutional rights or to conduct indiscriminate, wide-scale tracking. DHS removed it from its website in February 2025 without publicly explaining the change.

A separate policy required DHS mobile applications to collect personally identifiable or biometric information only when directly necessary for a department mission and documented through the privacy review process. DHS archived it around the same time.

Eight claims accuse DHS and its components of violating the Administrative Procedure Act, failing to perform mandatory duties under the Privacy Act, and retaliating against the three women for protected First Amendment activity.

The plaintiffs want the court to invalidate the alleged policy, restore the rescinded safeguards, and order DHS to delete photographs, video, license information, and vehicle records gathered solely because people engaged in lawful protest or observation.

They also seek to bar the government from using such information to deny Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or other benefits.

text:
US deports Kenyan former NFL player Daniel Adongo

A former NFL player from Kenya was deported last month by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency said, citing an overstayed visa, multiple arrests and prison time.

Daniel Adongo, 37, who was a linebacker for the Indianapolis Colts for two years, overstayed his visa in 2016, the year after his NFL career ended, according to the US authorities.

In a statement on Saturday, ICE - which dubbed him a "dangerous individual" - said he was ordered to leave the US on 23 March, and was removed from the country on 20 June.

Adongo, a rugby player at the time, made headlines in 2013 when he switched to American football in the US, having never taken part in the sport before.

"Those who violate immigration law are held equally accountable, including former professional athletes," ICE Chicago assistant field office director Douglas Thompson said.

"This dangerous individual was clearly a threat to the community, which is now safer since he's been removed."

Adongo has made no comment on the allegations against him and it is not clear where he was deported to.

According to the ICE statement, the former sportsman had been arrested "multiple times" over the past 10 years "for crimes including felony intimidation, battery and disorderly conduct".

His post-NFL life also saw him spend time in a psychiatric hospital, according to US newspaper the Indianapolis Star.

His mother and lawyers have been quoted as saying that he suffered from mental illness and injury, possibly from his time as an athlete.

In 2017 - after being charged with intimidation and criminal mischief - the newspaper said a judge ordered a psychiatric examination of Adongo to determine if he was capable of standing trial; he was ruled incompetent and was sent to a psychiatric hospital.

The trial was rescheduled multiple times including for not passing another psychiatric examination.

Then in 2020, he was convicted of "criminal mischief with damage", and sentenced to 364 days in prison, ICE said.

The agency added that his most recent charges fell under the US's Laken Riley Act, which requires undocumented immigrants, who are arrested for theft or violent crimes, to be held in prison pending trial.

US President Donald Trump signed the bill into law on 29 January, 2025, shortly after starting his second term.

The bill was named after Laken Riley - a Georgian nursing student who was murdered by a Venezuelan man a year earlier.

More than 40 Kenyans have been arrested by ICE, according to the US Department of Homeland Security website.

title: He was shot at by ICE, then wrongfully accused. His nightmare had only just begun - The Guardian

text:
It was just after 8am on 16 August and Francisco Longoria, who runs a party supply business, was driving his truck down a suburban southern California street to deliver a jumper for a water slide. But this ordinary Saturday morning turned into a nightmare when, suddenly, three unmarked vehicles stopped his truck and four masked men jumped out.

Longoria, who had brought his son Jonathan Longoria and son-in-law Daniel Rascon with him, wondered if they were being abducted.

“I see what happens in Mexico,” he said in Spanish. “I thought, are we going to be kidnapped by these masked men?”

The masked men were agents with US immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). They wore police gear, but Longoria said they didn’t identify themselves. As the agents walked toward the truck with their guns drawn, the passengers pulled out their phones to record video.

One agent pulled on the door handle, knocked on the window, and told Longoria to roll down his window, but the agent didn’t have a warrant. When Longoria didn’t comply, the agent smashed the glass and struck him in the face. Another agent broke the front passenger’s window.

With the agents on either side of the truck, and the road ahead clear, Longoria hit the gas. As he drove away, an agent shot three rounds, leaving two bullet holes in the passenger’s side of the truck. One bullet barely missed the back window. Sitting in the back seat, Rascon felt terrified. “One of us is about to get killed,” he thought.

“I was afraid for my life,” Longoria said. “I felt like death was imminent.”

The whole encounter lasted less than a minute, but it was only the beginning of the family’s harrowing tale.

The shooting happened a few blocks away from their home in San Bernardino, about 60 miles east of Los Angeles. When they arrived back at home minutes later, they called the police to report that masked men had shot at them.

Instead of receiving help, Longoria found himself in the crosshairs of a US government investigation that culminated in a night-time ambush of the family’s home, a felony charge accusing Longoria of weaponizing his vehicle against officers, and months in ICE detention – only for the case against him to eventually be dropped.

Longoria is speaking out for the first time as his family seeks justice for the violence they experienced. The family has filed a lawsuit against the federal government and the officers involved, seeking damages for physical injury, psychological injuries including PTSD, lost wages, property damages, wrongful incarceration, public humiliation and reputational harm.

The lawsuit alleges the officer “attempted to kill” them by firing shots in violation of CBP’s use of force policy, which directs officers to not shoot at “a moving vehicle merely fleeing from agents”; the only exception is if the agent has a reasonable belief that deadly force is being used against them or others present. “No legitimate law-enforcement purpose justified the use of deadly force under these circumstances,” the lawsuit states. It also alleges that the officers violated a temporary restraining order issued by a California judge that prohibited officers from targeting people solely based on race, language or type of work.

Longoria said he didn’t know why the agents stopped his truck, but suspects it was racial profiling. He and his family remain traumatized by their experience. “What I have lived through, I don’t wish that upon others,” he said.

The incident came at a tense time in their quiet neighborhood in San Bernardino, a predominantly Latino city with a population of more than 200,000 people. About a quarter of residents were born outside the US.

Elected on promises of an immigration crackdown, the Trump administration had ordered a string of aggressive immigration raids across the US. Southern California was an early target, as federal agents arrested more than 4,000 people from June to August last year, with immigrant advocates saying people were targeted based on their skin color, accents or jobs. Federal officers have routinely used excessive force, resulting in injuries and deaths, including the killings of Rene Good and Alex Pretti.

Longoria’s experience is not an isolated one. Since Trump took office last year, ICE has opened fire on at least 30 people, according to Trace, a US outlet tracking such shootings. However, after its agents act violently, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE and CBP, frequently accuses the victims of weaponizing their vehicles against officers. In many cases, such charges end up being dismissed.

This month, ICE agents shot and killed two men in their vehicles in Texas and Maine. Following the shootings, ICE paused most vehicle stops – a move swiftly reversed by Trump.

The Longoria family’s lawyers are calling on the California attorney general, Rob Bonta, to open a criminal investigation. “It was an illegal stop,” said Greg Jackson, partner and managing attorney at the Simon Law Group. “It’s one of those stops where they saw brown people in a truck and decided to exercise their perceived authority over them.”

DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s detailed request for comment about the Longoria family’s lawsuit and Longoria’s allegations about the shooting before publication.

Longoria, a chatty man with a green thumb who was born in Mexico, has spent the last 24 years planting roots in Southern California. He and his wife own a single-story home in San Bernardino, where they live with their children and son-in-law. The walls of their home are decorated with graduation and quinceañera photos, and a crucifix hangs next to the front door. Longoria, a devout Catholic, supported his family with his party rental business, while also working warehouse and restaurant shifts.

On the day of the shooting, Longoria arrived home and immediately called 911. When San Bernardino police arrived, he thought they were there to help. But he did not know that before he called, federal officers had already reported to local police that they shot at the truck. Call logs show that San Bernardino police misheard federal agents and believed Longoria had returned fire at them, so local police considered him a suspect, although they knew federal officers were not hit. “Marshal was not struck, med aid will be for a scrape to the arm,” the call logs state.

Local police arrived at Longoria’s home and arrested him. “They handcuffed me and put me in the car,” he said. They asked him if he ran over anyone with his truck, and he said no. His family members showed them the videos they had recorded.

While Longoria was in the squad car, the masked federal agents who had stopped the truck arrived at the family home. Local police looked up Longoria’s criminal record, but he didn’t have one. They had no reason to hold him.

But after local police released Longoria, ICE and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents attempted to arrest him themselves, telling family members to open the metal gate to their front yard. The agents lacked a warrant, so the family refused.

On the typically quiet street, neighbors noticed the heavy police presence. They poured out of their homes to defend Longoria and his family, who were known in the community for their contributions to the local church and party business.

The standoff between the crowd and police lasted several hours. Police call logs described the crowd as “hostile”. Officers deployed pepper spray and arrested several people.

Longoria said it felt good to see the community support: “I am forever indebted to them.”

When the officers left, the family felt relieved, but still on edge. They struggled to sleep for weeks after. Rascon noticed vehicles parked nearby that he believed were watching their home. Longoria stayed inside while family members, who are US citizens, picked up groceries and went to work. “We were still looking over our shoulders,” Rascon said.

It turned out their fears were justified. On 28 August, a security camera captured the moment at 4.19am when a group of federal officers in helmets, vests and night-vision goggles arrived while the family were still asleep, pointing guns at their door. They announced over a megaphone that they had a warrant for Longoria’s arrest.

Rascon was asleep on the couch when his mother-in-law shook him awake. He stood up and saw the agents outside carrying assault rifles. The family gathered in the living room, wearing the clothes they had been sleeping in, and called their lawyers.

The officers broke the locks on the exterior metal door and interior wooden door, and pointed assault rifles at them, the lasers from the guns hitting their bodies. Longoria said the agents told them: “If you move, we will shoot you.”

The lasers touched Joana Longoria, Rascon’s fiance, who was five months pregnant. Rascon told the officers: “Don’t shoot, she’s pregnant!”

“I was afraid of having a miscarriage [as a result of the stress],” she said.

The agents wanted to arrest Longoria, but the family shielded him. Longoria told them to step aside, fearing they would be killed. But Rascon said they refused to move until the officers produced a warrant.

The agents handed them a piece of paper that alleged Longoria had run over two officers with his vehicle, amounting to a felony charge of assault against federal officers with a dangerous weapon. The family’s lawyers confirmed over the phone that the warrant was legitimate, and they reluctantly allowed the agents to take Longoria. He wore only a muscle shirt and shorts, so they ran to get his clothes as the agents barked at them to hurry up. “I had to leave with my shoes in my hands,” Longoria said.

Jackson, the family’s attorney, said the ambush involved “extreme levels of violence that you would see for drug dealers, narco- terrorists, criminals” – an unnecessary amount of force for someone with no criminal history. He said DHS knew the family were represented by attorneys and could have contacted them with the warrant, avoiding the trauma of arresting him at gunpoint.

That same day, Longoria had a bond hearing. More than 30 community members filed into the courtroom. He felt blessed to see them, but frustrated about the felony charge. “Why is this happening to me?” he wondered. “I haven’t done anything wrong.”

During the hearing, the US attorney acknowledged he couldn’t think of a lawful basis for the officers to stop Longoria’s truck, and he wasn’t aware of any injuries to the officers. The judge said the videos recorded inside the truck were “quite scary”, and granted Longoria bond. But he was still subject to an ICE detainer, a request to hold a person so the agency can assume custody, because the government charged Longoria with being in the US without authorization.

The judge allowed him to hug his children before ICE took him. A few days later, he arrived at the Adelanto ICE facility, a massive 2,000-person capacity detention center in southern California’s high desert.

The food was awful, the portions were too small, and they weren’t given enough water, Longoria said. He estimated he lost 20lbs. The guards watched them constantly, even when they used the bathroom.

In Adelanto, he met people who were captured in the southern California raids – car-wash workers, street vendors, and day laborers. “The majority of people detained were hard-working people,” he said.

People who had been injured by federal agents showed him their broken hands and limbs, and he said they did not receive medical attention. At least two people died in Adelanto while he was there – Gabriel Garcia-Aviles, 56, and Ismael Ayala-Uribe, 39 – after ICE allegedly neglected their medical needs.

The government dropped the charges against Longoria on 17 September, but he was still held at Adelanto for a total of three months. After his lawyers fought for his release, Longoria returned home in early December – in time to celebrate Christmas and attend the birth of his granddaughter in January.

In February, Rascon testified before a House and Senate hearing examining violent abuses by DHS agents. “They’re terrorizing more than just our neighborhood … They haven’t stopped, to this day,” Rascon told the Guardian. He wants to see the officers face justice: “They should be imprisoned or charged.”

The lawsuit alleges officers attempted to “cover up” the truth of the shooting by making false statements that led Francisco to be charged – “part of a wide-ranging pattern of behavior … where ICE and/or CBP officers shoot or otherwise attack innocent people and then manufacture charges … falsely alleging the innocent individual ‘weaponized’ their vehicle, only to later dismiss all charges”.

Longoria doesn’t have bad wishes toward the officers – he only asks that they follow the law. “Instead, what they do is they injure people first, or kill them, and then later they figure out that they are good people,” he said.

Longoria, who is still facing removal proceedings from the US, wears an ankle monitor and regularly checks in with immigration authorities. He can’t work, so the rest of the family are working longer hours. Longoria is caring for his granddaughter Delilah, a calm baby with big, curious eyes who has brought them a renewed sense of joy.

With more time at home, Longoria has planted tomatoes, squash, watermelon, chilis and peas in every available inch of soil. But reminders of the family’s ordeal remain; the front door that was broken in the ambush has been nailed back together. His truck with the bullet holes and smashed windows is parked next to the house, unrepaired.

Longoria’s attorneys are fighting to keep him in the US.

“We will continue to go to court and see what happens next,” he said. “I want to stay in the country with my family, but I’m not the one to decide that. Only God can decide what happens to my future.”

text:
The government has decided to suspend refugee registration by the UN’s refugee agency (UNHCR). It simultaneously announced that around 5,000 Myanmar nationals will be returned to Myanmar.

Amnesty International Malaysia’s spokesperson, Divya Shesshsan Balakrishnan, responded: “While we welcome the government’s efforts to develop a national refugee registration system and move towards formal recognition of refugees in Malaysia, any transition away from UNHCR registration must not leave refugees and asylum-seekers without access to protection procedures.

“The timing of these announcements also raises serious questions. While UNHCR is being instructed to suspend refugee registrations, the government is simultaneously preparing to return approximately 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently held in immigration detention,” she said.

“Given the ongoing conflict and human rights situation in Myanmar, the government must be transparent about how these individuals were assessed, whether they were given a genuine opportunity to establish protection needs, and what safeguards are in place to ensure that no one is returned to a situation where they may face persecution or other serious human rights violations.

“As people in Myanmar continue to face forced labour, food and health crises, severe restrictions on movement, and an escalating armed conflict, any repatriation to the country at this time could have devastating consequences,” she added.

“Far from seeing conditions improve, people continue to undertake perilous journeys to flee Myanmar. Just last week, 500 people were feared dead after two boats carrying mostly Rohingya refugees capsized off the coast of Myanmar.

“The fact that people are still risking their lives to escape should be a stark reminder for Malaysia and all neighbouring countries that conditions in Myanmar remain unsafe,” she said.

“Malaysia should immediately clarify how asylum seekers are to seek protection while UNHCR registration is suspended, provide transparency on the assessment processes applied to those facing deportation, and ensure that no one is returned before their protection needs have been fully and fairly assessed.”

Background

On 23 July, Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni announced in Parliament that the government had directed the UNHCR to temporarily suspend refugee registration while Malaysia restructures refugee management through the ‘refugee registration document’ (DPP) programme.

He added that about 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently held in immigration detention are expected to be returned to Myanmar.

The DPP programme forms part of Malaysia’s plans to establish a government-led refugee registration and management system.

Under the programme, the government will collect refugee data, conduct identity verification and refugee status determination, and issue government-recognised documentation to successful applicants.

According to UNHCR figures cited in a recent parliamentary select committee report, Malaysia hosts 214,079 refugees and asylum seekers, some 90% of whom are from Myanmar. Around 31% are children.

The same report noted that 65% of refugee children are not enrolled in formal education.

According to a parliamentary reply dated 22 July, there were 22,166 migrants held in immigration detention facilities nationwide as of 30 June. Myanmar nationals constituted the largest group, accounting for 11,194 detainees.

Amnesty International Malaysia remains concerned that any transition from UNHCR registration to a national registration framework must ensure continuous access to protection procedures and robust safeguards against refoulement, particularly given the ongoing conflict and human rights crisis in Myanmar. – Amnesty Malaysia

text:
Governor Josh Stein is forcefully pushing back against federal plans to build a massive immigration detention facility in Eastern North Carolina.

Internal federal documents reveal that Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to turn the shuttered Rivers Correctional Institution in Winton into a 1,400-bed detention center. The move would create one of the largest ICE hubs on the East Coast, sparking immediate protests from civil rights advocates.

In a sharp public response, Governor Stein stated that while violent criminals here illegally should be deported, ICE has a track record of abuse and hasn't earned public trust. Because the facility is privately owned by the GEO Group, federal officials do not need state approval to open it. Local residents remain split, with some protesting the center and others welcoming the promise of 300 rural jobs.

Federal officials have not yet announced an official opening date for the facility.
