text:
Dozens turn out to express opposition at Saturday demonstration organized by ORD2 Indivisible

By Debora Gordon for Ashland.news

About 75 people used spoken word, song and signs Saturday, July 25, on Ashland Plaza to object to ongoing actions by federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

Criticism of ICE officers carrying out the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown have spiked again following back-to-back fatal shootings of immigrants in Maine on July 13 and in Texas on July 7.

The Oregon District 2 Indivisible organizers of the “ICE Out” event encouraged people to “come together to mourn the recent losses of human life at the hands of ICE and remind our community that we do not accept these acts of violence against our neighbors.”

Attendees interviewed at the rally are identified here only by their first names in accordance with their expressed preferences, apparently out of concern about having their full names known by authorities.

Dicke is among the majority of attendees interviewed who heard about the event through ORD2 Indivisible, describing it as a “worthy cause.”

“Of all the horrible things (President) Trump is doing,” Dicke said, “the worst is (to) drag … innocent people from their families, putting them in detention. We’ve never seen anything like this in America. These people are thugs. …

“People will keep pushing back, because the only way we’re going to beat this man is to resist and stand up to him, because he’s a bully, and if you stop him, you can maybe turn this around.”

Several participants, most of whom were old enough to remember protests of the 1960s and ‘70s, opined that there is a lot of backsliding in hard-won rights going on, noting women’s rights and voting rights are in the crosshairs.

Some said those in power are attempting to turn the U.S. into a white Christian male country.

Julie said she was invited via email.

“I live right down the street,” Julie said, “and I feel like it’s important to show up here at the Plaza, and make our voices heard,” adding that she has been attending other events, “Continuously, ever since Mr. Trump got elected.”

Ashland resident Tom is a member of and was invited by the Langston Hughes Affinity Group, which is affiliated with the United Church of Christ, and ORD2 Indivisible, “It’s also been well publicized. We are here to try and make our thoughts known, and to try and give democracy much more of a chance to prevail.” If he could speak directly to Trump, Tom would say, “Quit the corruption, and… make America free. ICE is still violating our rights. They’re going after lots of people. stand up, and it makes me think of World War II. Each human being has inherent dignity and worth. And I want him to remember that.

Ellen, a Talent resident and member of ORD2 Indivisible, decided to attend the vigil, “because I just find it horrifying what I see agents are doing to our neighbors, our friends, our community members, and it’s illegal, what they’re doing. And what I would say to Trump is ‘shame on you.’”

Medford resident Claudia also found out about the event through ORD2 Indivisible. She came “to see what I could possibly do,” she said. If she could speak directly to Trump, she would tell him, “We want democracy. Democracy demands voting, voting is part of democracy, and you are trying to subvert voting. This is unacceptable, and it’s causing a lot of distress for those of us in your country.”

Regarding ICE, Claudia added, “Immigrants are the backbone of our country. Without immigrants, we wouldn’t have a country. Most of us are immigrants.”

Cyd also came from Medford. She came to the event, she said, “Because I am so upset with ICE. I am so upset watching people just grabbed off the street. I feel like we’re falling into things I never imagined. And I have a lot of brown friends who are American citizens who are terrified.

“And a lot of people are in the process, and they’re still getting deported. And then I have friends that are worried that he’s going to rescind their citizenship. ICE to me looks like a shadow army. It’s terrifying to me. I just think it’s very serious. I can’t believe people aren’t more up in arms about it.”

Terrie Martin stepped into a leadership position with ORD2 Indivisible after joining, “About 10 years ago,” she explained, “when Trump was elected the first time. I was looking for a way to make a difference.

“And the wonderful thing about Indivisible is that you stand up and you hold your members of Congress accountable, because you can stand all day with a sign about Mr. Trump on an Ashland sidewalk, but he’s never going see it, and that’s how I got involved, because it is, I felt, a very effective way to resist.”

Saturday’s rally, she added, was called after “Indivisible national asked us to do a weekend of action this weekend, centered on the Hispanic people that have been killed by ICE, or harmed by ICE in the past month or so. They want to bring attention to that, and the fact that we’re standing up across the nation. We stand up for justice. We have a community protection team that works to watch the ICE building in Medford, for example, and to report ICE activity.”

As the gathering burgeoned, participants were invited to sing classic protest songs, including “”One Foot/Lead with Love” and “Down by the Riverside.”

Participants were invited to suggest new call and response lines for each of the songs, which included words and phrases such as “commitment,” “peace” and ended with “Ain’t Gonna Study War No More.”

Debora Gordon is a writer, artist, educator and non-violence activist who moved to Ashland from Oakland, California. Email her at debora.ashlandnews@gmail.com.

text:
Hong Kong Watch is renewing its call on the Home Office to immediately reverse course and allow Wu Chi-wai, the former Hong Kong Democratic Party chairman and one of the ‘Hong Kong 47,’ to remain in the UK with his wife and son, after new reporting revealed he faces removal this Wednesday. Hong Kong Watch previously raised concerns over Wu’s case after he was threatened with deportation on arrival at Heathrow Airport.

According to an Associated Press interview with Wu, he was finally able to embrace his wife and son in London last week for the first time since his release from prison, a reunion both he and his family had waited more than five years for. However, under his seven-day immigration bail granted on arrival, he is now due to leave the UK on Wednesday.

Wu told the AP he had taken care to inform Hong Kong’s British consulate of his travel plans beforehand, precisely because he was worried his “criminal” record might complicate his entry. Despite this, border officials at Heathrow apparently suspected he might be seeking long-term residency rather than a family visit, and he was only admitted on strict temporary bail. Wu has explicitly denied that he is seeking asylum in the UK, telling the AP his long-term hope is simply to reunite with his family there. He also said his return flight to Hong Kong, originally booked for November, has already been changed to Wednesday, and not by him. Neither the Home Office nor the airline had responded to questions about who altered the ticket.

Benedict Rogers, Chair and co-founder of Hong Kong Watch, said:

“Wu Chi-wai spent more than five years in prison for helping organise a primary election. His reward should not be a week with his wife and son before being put back on a plane. The Home Office says it is ‘steadfast’ in supporting Hong Kongers. Now is the moment to prove it, by allowing Mr Wu to stay.

It is hard to see how a man who had already told the UK government, in writing, ahead of time, exactly why he was travelling, ends up on immigration bail with a week’s notice to leave. Over 200,000 Hong Kongers have settled in the UK under the BN(O) route in good faith, trusting that Britain’s offer of sanctuary is real. Every day this case goes unresolved, that trust is tested. The Home Office must extend Wu’s leave to remain, and explain what went wrong.”

text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wouldn’t rule out a vote to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement if Democrats retake the House, but downplayed the push for the move from within his own party.

“I’ve spoken to several of the incoming members of Congress across the ideological spectrum,” Jeffries (D-NY) told CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday.. “Not a single person has raised those issues other than, obviously, what they’ve seen from House Democrats in pushing back against an out-of-control ICE.

“We believe that immigration enforcement in this country clearly should be fair, just and humane. And that’s not what’s taking place,” the top House Democrat went on, calling for ICE agents to “conduct themselves like every other cop, police officer and law enforcement agent in the country.”

Numerous Democrats running for House seats in the 2026 midterm cycle on a platform that includes outright abolishing ICE.

Zohran Mamdani-backed candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, who recently bested Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-NY) in a primary last month, has called for abolishing ICE and scrubbed past social media posts about abolishing prisons — a position she has yet to clearly disavow.

Jeffries boasted about how Democrats have resisted funding ICE without serious reforms to the immigration enforcement agency, something that led to multiple government shutdowns earlier this year.

The ICE fight has also complicated government funding for the next fiscal year, which starts on Oct. 7. House Republicans passed a measure last week to prevent a government shutdown, but it hasn’t yet gotten through the Senate.

“House Democrats have taken a strong position as it relates to not giving a dime to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine until, of course, there is dramatic reform in this country,” Jeffries crowed.

At one point, the Democratic leader was pressed about a CNN report about him and Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY) battling Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) over his meddling in a primary involving a black Democrat.

Sanders had backed Nida Allam in her unsuccessful March primary against incumbent Rep. Valerie Foushee (D-NC).

“No, I wouldn’t describe it as a clash. It was a candid conversation, along with Congressman Greg Meeks, the chair of the Congressional Black Caucus PAC, with respect to one particular race in North Carolina,” Jeffries said.

“I do think that Senator Sanders and Democrats in both the House and the Senate understand the stakes that are in front of us, particularly as we are 100 days out, and that’s making sure that we actually take back control of the Congress, so we can end this MAGA extremism,” he added.

title: Closed Borders and Denied Rights. Migrants in Mexico in 'Legal Limbo' - la civiltà cattolica
description:
Recognized as the main migration hub in the Americas, Mexico has seen an exponential increase in the number of countries from which migrants originate over the past 10 years.
Currently, the migration situation in Mexico has undergone a significant change.
In your work in Mexico, you meet people from many different countries, each with their own stories and needs.
What is the public’s perception, and what measures have the authorities taken to support migrants and refugees?
For this reason, our support efforts have focused on mental health and legal issues, but with a particular emphasis on community integration.
text:
It is one of the 10 countries in the world with the highest number of people seeking refuge, and due to the tightening of U.S. immigration policies, it is shifting from a transit country to a place where thousands of people are stranded in a sort of “legal limbo,” exposed to violence from organized crime and lacking adequate safety nets. Recognized as the main migration hub in the Americas, Mexico has seen an exponential increase in the number of countries from which migrants originate over the past 10 years. However, the lack of reception facilities and long waiting times often make it impossible to meet even basic needs, such as food, shelter and health care.

This situation echoes words Pope Leo XIV recently addressed to organizations working to welcome migrants on the Canary Islands, at the conclusion of his apostolic journey to Spain. “Human dignity demands legal and safe pathways, rescue and assistance, real cooperation against traffickers, effective protection for victims, serious processes of reception and integration, and policies that allow every person to live with dignity in their own land,” the Holy Father stated. “While there is a right to seek refuge when life is threatened, there is also the right not to have to migrate: the right to remain in one’s own home without hunger, war, persecution, violence, the land becoming uninhabitable, corruption stealing bread from the poor, weapons destroying the future of children. We cannot grow accustomed to counting the dead. Human dignity has no passport and does not lose its value when crossing a border.”[1]

In this complex migration landscape, the Jesuit Refugee Service (JRS) is committed to supporting migrants and asylum seekers by providing them with humanitarian aid, legal assistance, and pathways to integration into local communities.

How has the migration phenomenon changed in recent years, and what are the main challenges the country faces today? We asked Karen Vanessa Pérez Martínez, head of the national office of JRS Mexico.

Currently, the migration situation in Mexico has undergone a significant change. We are talking about people who find themselves in an unstable situation with regard to their life plans, and this is linked to the closure of the border between Mexico and the United States. Although this development has not stopped the flow of people arriving at the borders or within the country, these individuals find themselves in a legal limbo, lacking support networks and in need of international protection. At the same time, Mexico continues to be one of the top 10 countries hosting the largest number of people seeking refuge due to various circumstances, such as the risks they face in their countries of origin.

Among the main challenges we face is the complete lack of response from the immigration authorities responsible for facilitating procedures, such as asylum applications and, of course, security issues. Mexico is experiencing a serious crisis involving enforced disappearances which, combined with the high costs of being a migrant in various regions and the presence of organized crime and criminal groups, has led to many people becoming victims of severe violence. All of this is taking place against a backdrop of support networks being dismantled; in particular, we are referring to human rights organizations, which have been severely affected by cuts to their funding.

In your work in Mexico, you meet people from many different countries, each with their own stories and needs. Has the number of countries of origin increased over the years? Are there specific vulnerabilities among migrants and asylum seekers?

Yes, over the past 10 years, the exponential increase in the number of countries of origin has become a matter of great significance, especially in light of the cultural and linguistic challenges. We have identified over 110 nationalities from all over the world; however, those arriving from Africa, Asia, the Middle East, the Caribbean, and Central America have a greater need for international assistance. It is important to emphasize that there are many vulnerabilities among the people arriving at the country’s various borders: these individuals face discrimination, xenophobia and mistreatment, and receive little or no assistance due to the high number of people and the multitude of needs present. The lack of reception facilities, job opportunities, and long waiting times make it impossible to provide food, shelter and basic healthcare. There are people who, due to their precarious situation, go without food for the entire day. This affects both migrants and asylum seekers.

In recent months, immigration policies along the border between Mexico and the United States have become stricter. What consequences do these measures have on people’s lives? Are they effective in discouraging people from leaving? And what impact are they having on migration routes?

It is important to emphasize that the main consequences are on their mental and physical health: people have experienced highly stressful situations, including unemployment, a lack of safe places to live, and violence that results in exposure to criminal groups and forced disappearances; the impact is enormous. People find themselves rethinking their life plans; a sense of fear about the near future prevails among them, and as this happens, they prefer to remain in Mexico, even if they are deported. We are faced with a narrative that has been echoed by everyone who has had to return from the north to the south, with a clear message: “DO NOT CROSS THE BORDER; THERE IS NO PASSAGE.” This has undoubtedly had an impact on Mexico in terms of an increase in asylum requests, the ongoing and growing militarization of the borders, rising violence along the routes, as well as the search for new ways to move within the country.

How is Mexico responding to this new situation? What is the public’s perception, and what measures have the authorities taken to support migrants and refugees?

Those of us dealing with this situation have tried to respond as best we can, since we find ourselves in a vulnerable position, alone and grappling with budget cuts that have had a very severe impact on our work: we’ve been forced to close offices, scale back services, shut down shelters, distribute less food, deal with more red tape, and so on. We decided to organize ourselves as we have done in other emergencies, to listen to one another and reflect on how we could respond, identify the most pressing needs, and coordinate among those who can still care for people. People have shared with us their emotional distress and the changes to their plans, largely due to the fear of setting foot on U.S. soil; these same people have begun seeking ways to integrate into their communities. For this reason, our support efforts have focused on mental health and legal issues, but with a particular emphasis on community integration. People have chosen to remain in Mexico and begin their applications, but also to wait for changes in the neighboring country’s immigration policy.

In a recent issue of La Civiltà Cattolica, we quoted the statement by the U.S. bishops on migrants from November 2025: “We bishops advocate for ameaningful reform of our nation’s immigration laws and procedures. Human dignity and national security are not in conflict.” Is it possible today to reform immigration laws and procedures while respecting human dignity?

It is possible, provided that all parties are willing. In fact, the legal framework presents many challenges and gray areas that require a concrete, practical and humane interpretation, since the migration issue weighs heavily on countries, and even more so in Mexico. The number of people who have applied for asylum is very high, and the response has been very limited. As for the procedures, it seems to me that much of what has been said about respect for human dignity is particularly significant when people find themselves overwhelmed by complex situations precisely because of the application of these very same immigration procedures carried out by the competent authorities.

JRS Mexico describes its mission as being based on three verbs: accompanying, serving and defending. How are these principles put into practice in the day-to-day assistance provided to people on the move?

The support we have been providing for many years has always been based on a fundamental principle: placing people at the center in a dignified and respectful manner; in other words, our daily care has evolved according to each person’s abilities, schedule and needs. We strive to provide people with all the tools they need to make the best decisions for their life plans, with full awareness and by leveraging what we can offer within our support networks. Currently, we have focused on comprehensive support that allows us to accompany people on their legal journeys, as well as their personal ones, with empathy, in the certainty that our support is precisely this opportunity to give space to each individual; even in the midst of crises, creating community and building it together has allowed us to understand and navigate reality with the skills and resources at our disposal; even if these are limited, our commitment is not.

In addition to humanitarian and legal assistance, JRS invests heavily in community integration. Why is it so important to support people even after the emergency has passed, and what results are you seeing?

JRS in Mexico has weathered numerous migration crises, and throughout them, we have seen how essential it is to integrate people into the community, not only because so many have now decided to stay, but also because this has allowed us to support processes that, over the years, have transformed the lives of many people. For us, supporting these processes has meant learning from the people themselves, observing how they manage to develop their own abilities. For us, carrying out projects that create spaces and ensure access to services, education and economic inclusion has inspired others to join in concrete actions. The fact that this is the right path is evident in the resilience shown, in the creation of opportunities, and in the building of a community that sees its own capacities strengthened. And for us, this is truly incredible.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will be reopening a for-profit prison in Winton, North Carolina, as one of the largest immigrant detention facilities on the East Coast, according to reports from the New York Times.

The report cited internal ICE documents showing plans for a mass detention center in the former Rivers Correctional Institution with 1,400 beds. It’s part of an agreement between the federal government and GEO Group, a nationwide private prison network.

On its website, GEO Group recently published a job posting for a “facility maintenance manager” for Rivers Correctional Institution, a prison that has been empty for five years. A separate recruiting website lists the posting date as July 11.

GEO Group previously operated the facility as a “criminal alien requirement” prison, reserved for non-citizens convicted of federal crimes, before the U.S. terminated its contract in 2021.

During its years of operation from 2001 to 2021, Rivers was the subject of a litany of health and safety complaints from inmates who alleged understaffing, inadequate medical care, and pervasive discrimination by staff.

In a 2007 class action lawsuit, inmates incarcerated at Rivers alleged a pattern of denial of medical treatment that led to severe injury and death in some instances. “The health care system at the Rivers facility is broken,” the complaint alleged. GEO Group was ultimately dismissed from the lawsuit before those claims could be addressed.

GEO Group did not respond to a request for comment on the facility’s reopening.

A spokesperson for ICE said in a statement to NC Newsline that while the agency is at work expanding its capacity around the U.S., no new facility is opening yet.

“We have no new detention centers to announce at this time,” the agency said in a statement. “It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space.”

Kristi Graunke, the legal director for the ACLU of North Carolina, said the facility has been on her radar for months. The Washington Post reported last August that the federal government was considering reopening it, and apparent construction activity at the facility led to protests by advocates and local residents in recent months.

“We had an inkling that this would be looked at, and certainly we were also hearing from community partners who were essentially seeing signs that Rivers would be reopened in Winton,” Graunke said. “Construction equipment, trucks, heavy machinery — items that suggested that work was taking place there.”

Gov. Josh Stein condemned the facility’s reopening on social media Friday. He emphasized that the facility is not state-owned, and he had no role in its reopening as a detention facility.

“ICE has a proven track record of arresting, detaining, and abusing American citizens, and the overwhelming majority of people ICE has detained have no criminal record. Meanwhile, last year dozens of people died while in ICE custody,” Stein wrote. “Like many other North Carolinians, I do not want it in our state. ICE and Border Patrol have not earned our trust.”

While public backlash has been effective in halting some ICE initiatives — including a push to repurpose warehouses around the U.S. as mass detention centers — advocates say there is little local residents can do to block a facility that has already been built from reopening.

“All the permitting and all the stuff that local communities can typically rally around when these things are proposed already happened decades ago at Rivers,” said Andreina Malki, a defense manager at immigrant rights group Siembra NC. “That being said, if it’s going to be opened as a detention center, I think we need to make sure that local elected officials or other community representatives have access to the place.”

The Hertford County Board of Commissioners did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement on social media earlier this year, the county government stressed that it has no ability to intervene in the facility’s activities.

“The Rivers Correctional Facility is a privately operated facility that operates under contract with the federal government,” the county wrote in February. “Decisions regarding its use, operations, or repurposing are made at the federal level and are not under the authority or control of Hertford County Government or the Hertford County Board of Commissioners.”

Malki said advocates can still make a difference by opposing further ICE expansion in the state.

“One thing that we can do in North Carolina in general, beyond Winton or Hertford County, is make sure that in places where we don’t have prisons built already, where we don’t have detention centers built, which are not zoned for that kind of facility, that that doesn’t happen,” Malki said. “If there’s a town or a city, county that’s proposing something like that, be proactive so that this is the last detention center that we see open in North Carolina.”

A group of Venezuelan men who were sent to a notorious Central American prison by the Trump administration have filed a lawsuit against the aviation companies contracted to transport them from the United States to El Salvador.

According to The Guardian, the lawsuit was filed earlier this week in a Washington, D.C.-based federal court. It names defendants including CSI Aviation and GlobalX, which allegedly violated the men’s civil rights through false imprisonment, the intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligence, among other violations.

CSI and GlobalX, lawyers say, both went to “great lengths” to undertake the “rendition flights” to El Salvador, which were conducted “in concert with the U.S. government, in flagrant violation of U.S. and international law.”

The Guardian notes that, last year, the Trump administration expelled more than 230 Venezuelan men from the United States to El Salvador, where they were detained for up to four months in a maximum-security prison designed to house terrorists. The plaintiffs say they were there subjected to abuse, up to and including torture.

The lawsuit accuses CSI and GlobalX of deliberately transporting the men to El Salvador, despite a federal court ordering the flights to return and despite knowing that the men would likely be tortured upon arrival at the Terrorism Confinement Center, better known by its Spanish-language acronym, “CECOT.”

“Despite knowing that El Salvador’s Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo (‘CECOT’) mega-prison was a notorious blacksite, from which no detainee had ever left alive, Defendants went to great lengths to transport Plaintiffs and Class Members there, in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of U.S. and international law,” the lawsuit alleges. “Defendants evaded or ignored judicial oversight and the foreseeable risk of torture and successfully delivered Plaintiffs and the Class to El Salvador for imprisonment at CECOT.”

A November 2025 report issued by Human Rights Watch indicates that the men were probably “subjected to what amounts to arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance under international human rights law.” The same report also detailed inhumane conditions, torture, and an atmosphere tolerant of abuse, accusing guards of regularly beating, pepper-spraying, and sexually assaulting detainees.

The lawsuit says that the Venezuelan plaintiffs continue to struggle with the long-term physical and mental health effects of their confinement; CSI and GlobalX, in contrast, have allegedly “enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme and their relationship with the [Trump] Administration.”

text:
Loved ones of the San Francisco woman who was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at San Francisco International Airport earlier this week say they have received phone calls from her while she is being held at the California City ICE Detention Facility.

They said that after phone system issues throughout the day, they were able to get a call from her Saturday night, where she told them she is meeting other detainees at the facility who also live in San Francisco and were also arrested recently at airports, including at San Francisco International Airport.

Friends said this woman is Iryna Gorb, who has lived in San Francisco for 10 years and is known by many as a barista, photographer and friend.

"She works at a cafe called Better Half, she’s worked at a few others in her time here," said her friend Andy Eblin of San Francisco. Eblin said Gorb called him Wednesday evening from the Stockton ICE Field Office, where she told him she was taken immediately after her arrest. Since then, he said she has been taken to the California City Detention Facility.

Eblin has been able to receive several phone calls from Gorb in the days since, and has been working with a group of more than a dozen of her friends to coordinate logistical and legal support. He noted that the length of the allowed phone calls she can make varies significantly, and that for most of the day Saturday her calls did not go through.

"She would be the first one to want me to say, this is part of a bigger story," Eblin noted.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed to NBC Bay Area that they arrested Gorb, whom they identified as being from Ukraine, at SFO on Wednesday.

"When officers approached Gorb, she attempted to flee and resisted arrest," a DHS spokesperson said, adding that Gorb overstayed her visa by 15 years and will "remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings."

The arrest was captured on video Wednesday night at the Harvey Milk Terminal of SFO by Richmond City Council member Doria Robinson, showing Gorb screaming, pinned down on the ground by two men.

The men appear to be in plainclothes and did not respond in the video to questions from others in the airport about who they work with or why they are arresting her. Robinson said the men handcuffed Gorb and carted her away in a wheelchair.

That video has now been shared widely across many accounts and news outlets on social media.

"That video has helped a ton with attention," said Eblin, "it's impossible for me to watch, but without it, we wouldn’t have had the response we’ve had."

NBC Bay Area asked the Department of Homeland Security about the video and about why the officers are not seen wearing identifying clothing and did not respond to questions about who they work for.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson responded, "When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement."

Robinson maintains that at no point when she was recording the video or when she was in the terminal did she see the men wearing any identifying clothing. She also said she did not hear the men say who they worked for or what they were doing.

Gorb's friends said that she has many contacts in the arts and fashion community in San Francisco and that she had her own vintage shop out of a studio in the city for a while. Eblin said that when Gorb first called him from ICE custody, she told him to let her manager at the coffee shop know that she wouldn't be able to work and to let her friends know that she would be unable to watch their cats for them.

Gorb's case is getting focus from elected officials as well.

San Francisco Supervisor Danny Sauter described the video of her arrest as "sickening."

"I'm in touch with immigration lawyers and legal defense partners who are supporting Iryna," Sauter said. "She also has the strength of countless friends and neighbors who know her as the valued part of San Francisco that she is."

State Sen. Scott Wiener also condemned Gorb's arrest and said in a statement, "Iryna Gorb made a home in San Francisco and is one of many people who help make San Francisco run. She is part of our community."

Gorb's friends said they have been in touch with Wiener's office as well as the offices of other local elected officials, sharing concern about growing reports of ICE arrests at airports.

Several Bay Area immigration attorneys told NBC Bay Area that they have been hearing about an uptick in ICE arrests at airports in recent weeks and are advising clients not to fly.

Gorb's friends said she is working with an attorney and is making a petition for her release.

text:
As Election Day nears, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s record shows repeated support for efforts to secure the southern border.

Paxton has served as attorney general since 2015. Since then, he has consistently supported measures related to the Texas-Mexico border. He launched legal efforts to defend state laws related to crime and illegal immigration, and he won multiple federal court battles against the Biden administration.

In 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term, Paxton joined Trump at a roundtable discussion in McAllen, Texas, focused on border security. The meeting was intended to discuss conditions at the southern border and potential responses to illegal immigration.

In 2021, after President Joe Biden took office, Paxton continued filing lawsuits challenging the administration’s immigration policies.

After Biden suspended certain deportation actions, Paxton filed a complaint in 2021 seeking to halt the Department of Homeland Security’s freeze on removals.

In March of that year, he led a 14-state coalition before the U.S. Supreme Court in defense of a federal law prohibiting immigration by illegal aliens who are likely to rely on taxpayer-funded government programs. Months later, in July, Paxton won a ruling from a U.S. District Court judge that blocked the federal government from approving new applications under the Obama Administration’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program while litigation continued.

In August 2021, He obtained a preliminary injunction against the Biden administration related to the detention of certain noncitizens convicted of crimes. Before the year’s end, he asked a court to order the Biden administration to immediately resume construction of the southern border wall, arguing that the administration violated federal law by halting the use of congressionally appropriated funds for wall construction.

Paxton also helped secure a ruling in December 2021 that restored the “Remain in Mexico” program, which required immigrants seeking to enter the U.S. illegally to remain in Mexico until U.S. courts ruled on their immigration status.

In 2023, Paxton again prioritized border security through additional legal challenges against the Biden administration.

During a monthslong legal battle over Texas’ border barriers, Paxton won an injunction from the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that barred the federal government from damaging, destroying, or interfering with Texas’ concertina wire fencing along the southern border while litigation continued.

In November of that year, Paxton sent a letter to then-Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas stating that a newly enacted Texas law granted additional authority to law enforcement officers under certain circumstances.

Paxton continued pursuing border-related legal action after Biden left office. In June 2026, he obtained a Texas Supreme Court order temporarily freezing Harris County’s $1.3 million program that provided legal representation to illegal aliens facing deportation proceedings.

In April 2026, Paxton defended Senate Bill 4, which was passed during the 88th Texas Legislature and made illegal entry into Texas from a foreign nation a state crime while authorizing state law enforcement full authority to arrest and order the return of illegal aliens. Paxton sought and obtained a preliminary injunction in federal district court, which was later affirmed by the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

Additionally, Paxton issued a statement supporting House Resolution 50, sponsored by Republican U.S. Rep. Jodey Arrington of Texas, which affirms the constitutional authority of states to defend themselves against border invasions.

These and other actions won Paxton an endorsement by the National Border Patrol Council. In announcing the endorsement, council President Paul Perez said the organization believes Paxton “will continue fighting for the resources, policies, and leadership our agents need to keep America’s borders secure.”

Madison Cercy, Paxton’s campaign spokesperson, told the Daily Signal that he will continue fighting for Texans.

“Attorney General Ken Paxton leads the nation on border security. He sued the Biden Administration over 100 times to stop the flood of illegal immigration and protect Texas communities. He defended Texas’ right to secure the border, blocked unlawful parole programs, upheld our state border laws, and worked with law enforcement to take on the cartels exploiting the crisis at our southern border,” she said.

“As the next U.S. Senator from Texas, Paxton will fully fund President Trump’s border security agenda, finish securing the southern border, arm Border Patrol and law enforcement with the resources they need, crack down on the cartels flooding our streets with fentanyl and other deadly drugs, and support mandatory detention and deportation of dangerous criminal illegal immigrants.”

Election Day is Nov. 3

text:
A judgment has been made that the immigration enforcement act of presuming a foreign national with lawful residency status to be an undocumented foreigner and exercising force without verifying their identity constitutes a human rights violation.

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea announced on the 27th that it recently recommended an immigration office, whose officers restrained a foreigner by holding both hands without checking the person’s identity, to conduct internal work training. The commission specifically pointed out that staff performing immigration enforcement duties must receive training to comply with the basic principles of conduct, regulations for the use of protective equipment, and onsite documentation guidelines according to the Immigration Act and the human rights protection code of conduct during the enforcement process for immigration offenders.

The complainant, a diaspora Korean with valid residency status, filed a petition asserting that while working at a grocery store in June of last year, two immigration office employees unjustly exercised force by attempting to handcuff them without checking their identity or presenting any grounds for the enforcement. The immigration officers argued that the area near the incident site is known to have many undocumented foreign workers, and that they only restrained both of the complainant’s hands to prevent a safety accident because the complainant was working with a box cutter. They also explained that no actual handcuffing took place.

The Human Rights Commission reviewed the grocery store’s internal CCTV footage and confirmed that the immigration officers, without verifying the complainant’s residency status, restrained both hands from behind with handcuffs in their possession solely because the complainant was holding a box cutter. However, it was not proven through the CCTV whether the officers actually attempted to handcuff the individual.

The commission concluded that the problem lay in the fact that the immigration officers prematurely exercised force without identity verification or warning, having assumed the complainant to be an undocumented foreigner. The commission also found that immediately restraining the individual simply because they were holding a box cutter, without first following the minimum infringement principle, constituted an excessive response. Furthermore, the commission determined that such actions infringed on bodily freedom as guaranteed by the Constitution.

An official from the Human Rights Commission commented, “The officers should have first identified themselves as immigration officials, requested identification, and then determined whether the use of handcuffs or other force was warranted based on the complainant’s actions. Exercising force preemptively against a lawful resident who showed no intent to resist is inappropriate.”

text:
Gov. Ned Lamont and his top public safety official acknowledged Friday the presence of federal ICE agents at Bradley International Airport without being able to say if it signaled a new emphasis on immigration enforcement by the Trump administration in Connecticut.

“We were made aware that they are at the airport, and if someone goes through TSA, that they may be checked. And if in fact there’s a violation, that they’re pulled out of the line,” said Ronnell Higgins, the commissioner of emergency services and public protection. “But that’s the extent to what I know right now.”

The media offices of ICE in New England and nationally did not respond to a request for comment.

Connecticut is one of the blue states where immigration enforcement is a source of chronic conflict, given the passage of revisions to Trust Act that set explicit limits on the circumstances in which local enforcement can cooperate with the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.

“Connecticut State Police is assigned to Bradley Airport. They are not involved in any way” in the immigration enforcement there, Higgins said.

Higgins said ICE officially notified the state of its presence without sharing details on long-range plans. The federal agency does not routinely notify state police of arrests at the airport, a state-owned facility in Windsor Locks with federal oversight.

“I have no reason to believe that they’re going to not be there tomorrow or the next day or the next day,” Higgins said.

Lamont on Friday repeated the message he has been articulating since the opening of the General Assembly session in February.

“Leave us alone. Leave these people alone,” he said. “These are maybe people who want to go for a long weekend and see the aunt in Chicago, instead of getting picked up by ICE, the TSA at Bradley, maybe sent away to a detention facility. I don’t want to jump to conclusions. We’ll see what’s happening.”

State authorities could not confirm if anyone was arrested and detained at the airport by ICE.

The Connecticut Airport Authority released a statement about the ICE presence late Friday.

“The CAA has been made aware that ICE agents have conducted several targeted operations in recent weeks at Bradley International Airport,” the statement reads. “The federal agents involved wore plain clothes and were not readily identifiable as ICE agents. ICE appears to be carrying out similar operations at airports across the country. The CAA did not assist in these operations in any way and has learned of them only after the fact.

“The CAA has no authority to intervene or prevent such operations, which occurred predominantly in areas under the control of the federal government,” the statement continues. “The mission of the CAA is to provide the safest and most convenient facilities for our workforce and the many families and individuals traveling through Bradley International Airport, and this initiative does not further that mission.”

TRAC, the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, reported that more than 65,000 people were in immigration detention nationally as of July 11 and that 70% were individuals without criminal convictions.

text:
About 150 people gathered in downtown Mountain View Saturday evening as part of a nationwide day of action honoring two men shot and killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers earlier this month.

The vigil at Castro Street and El Camino Real featured live music from the Raging Grannies, a longtime Peninsula activist group known for using protest songs to promote social justice causes. Organizers described the gathering as both a protest against federal immigration enforcement and a space to grieve.

The gathering honored Lorenzo Salgado Araujo of Houston and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero of Maine, who were killed during separate ICE enforcement operations six days apart.

"It is more of a vigil because we need to grieve, right? We need to acknowledge these people," organizer Mariya Ganzo said. She helps lead Blue Turn Indivisible, a Mountain View-area advocacy group.

Ruth Robertson of the Raging Grannies said music has long been a way for the group to carry its activism beyond demonstrations.

"We've heard that people go home and sing these songs standing in their kitchen, and even little kids recite them, and so that is a way of spreading the word, and we love to do it that way," Robertson said.

Demonstrators held signs, sang protest songs and called for greater accountability over federal immigration enforcement.

ICE did not immediately respond to CBS News Bay Area's request for comment Saturday.

Federal authorities have defended the officers' actions in both shootings. ICE said Salgado Araujo tried to run over an officer during the July 7 operation in Houston before an agent opened fire. In Maine, the Department of Homeland Security said an officer fired on July 13 as Durán Guerrero tried to drive away because the officer feared for public safety. Both shootings remain under investigation.

Robertson said immigrants are living with fear as enforcement actions continue across the country.

"People are being targeted here, and are afraid. They're afraid to go out of their houses, they're afraid to go to work," she said.

For attendee Sheryl Stark, showing up was itself a meaningful act of civic participation.

"Call your senator, call your representative, things like that," Stark said. "But I think the most important thing and the least thing you can do, is to show up."

Robertson said Saturday's demonstration also reflected decades of activism by members of the Raging Grannies, some of whom first protested during the Vietnam War era.

"We were high school and college students at the time. So this is not new to us, although the situation was different, we are always on the side of justice," Robertson said.

Organizers said they plan to continue holding similar vigils and protests across the Bay Area in the coming weeks.

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s border czar said Sunday that the vetting of an immigration officer involved in the deadly shooting of a Colombian native in Maine is under internal review after relatives revealed to The Associated Press that he had a history of serious mental health struggles and violent behavior.

Tom Homan said if the allegations against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer are true, “I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting.”

“There’s several things under review,” Homan said on CNN about the officer, Army veteran David Brouillette. “The training is under review. I know this specific case, as far as the vetting, is under review by the internal affairs section.”

Questions about the Department of Homeland Security’s rush to hire, train and deploy thousands of new ICE officers to carry out Trump’s immigration crackdown have come into stark focus after back-to-back fatal shootings of immigrants in Maine and Houston.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ordered a pause in vehicle stops after the fatal Maine shooting, but Trump almost immediately reversed course and insisted the stops resume as a necessary tool in his campaign to round up and deport immigrants who are in the U.S. without current legal status.

Homeland Security did not immediately respond Sunday to a request for comment about the internal review.

ICE issues new requirement for body-worn cameras during vehicle stops

Homan said that “changes have been made” and that acting ICE director David Venturella has issued a new directive that body-worn cameras must be in use if officers make a vehicle stop.

“Right now, on all vehicle stops, there’s at least one body camera on site to record the entire event,” he said.

He said Venturella “sent an instruction out that he wants at least one body camera on those vehicle stops, so we have everything on video.”

It’s unclear if the steps that the department is taking will be enough to quell the concerns coming from certain lawmakers in Congress over Homeland Security’s training and tactics as tries to reach Trump’s mass deportation goals.

Lawmakers push for answers but have more questions

Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns.

Democrats pressed ICE officials during a closed-door briefing for the House Homeland Security Committee last week, leaving some with more questions than answers.

Lawmakers were told during the briefing that there have been 56 complaints of excessive force against ICE officers - 32 were cleared, and one was referred for disciplinary action.

No discipline had yet been handed out, the lawmakers said they were told. The rest of the incidents are still under investigation.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has pushed for the use of body-worn cameras and ensured funding for the effort. She had said it was “extremely unfortunate” that the officer involved in the shooting in her home state was not using a camera.

Homeland Security is under scrutiny but also faces pressure to increase deportations

The Trump administration has failed to meet its goal of deporting 1 million people a year, despite an intense immigration enforcement crackdown that has resulted in violent scenes in cities nationwide.

At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers since the start of Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

While the Trump administration insists it is targeting the “worst of the worst” criminals, that has not always been the result and American citizens also have been among the deaths.

The ICE officer shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian national who was killed in his car near his home in the coastal city of Biddeford.

In Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed July 7 when ICE officers chased his white work van through the streets, then shot him through the window in front of his work crew, including his brother.

Earlier this year, two Americans protesting ICE actions in Minneapolis, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old nurse, were killed, sparking a backlash nationwide.

Democrats launched the longest agency shutdown in history earlier this year when they refused to fund Homeland Security in a largely failed attempt to force the administration to impose various restraints on the officers.

If you feel like you need a law degree and a crystal ball just to fill out Form I-9 these days, you’re not wrong — and you’re not alone. Temporary Protected Status (TPS) has become one of the most volatile corners of immigration law in 2026, with the Supreme Court, multiple federal district courts, and the Department of Homeland Security all pulling in different directions on the same week sometimes. On June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court decided Mullin v. Doe, ruling that most legal challenges to TPS terminations can’t even be heard in court, which effectively handed DHS a green light to move fast on ending protections for hundreds of thousands of people. Since then, the dominoes have been falling — but not all at once, and not evenly, because a patchwork of district court stays is still (for now) keeping some EADs alive.

This post breaks down, country by country, what’s actually happening on the ground for employers as of July 24, 2026 — not the political noise, just the practical rules you need to follow to stay compliant.

The Big Picture: Why This Is So Messy Right Now

Here’s the state of play in a nutshell:

DHS has moved to terminate TPS for Ethiopia, Yemen, Burma, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, Haiti, and Venezuela, each through its own Federal Register notice.

Federal courts stepped in for most of these countries, issuing stays that (temporarily) kept work authorization alive while litigation played out.

Then came Mullin v. Doe. The Supreme Court held that Congress largely stripped courts of the power to second-guess DHS’s TPS decisions, which knocked out the main legal theory (the “arbitrary and capricious” argument under the Administrative Procedure Act) that had been blocking terminations for Burma, Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen, and others.

The lower courts haven’t all caught up yet. So right now, EADs for several of these countries are in a kind of legal purgatory — technically terminated, but still valid on paper because a district court order hasn’t been lifted.

And the volatility isn’t limited to our eight focus countries. On July 21, 2026, a federal court in Massachusetts temporarily blocked a separate USCIS policy — tied to the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — that would have cut short certain TPS holders’ 540-day automatic work authorization extensions effective July 22, 2026. That order (in Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts v. USCIS) mainly affects TPS holders from Ukraine, El Salvador, and Sudan, but it’s a fresh reminder that this landscape can shift overnight, even outside the eight countries covered in detail below.

Translation for HR: don’t assume anything is settled. What’s true today may not be true in ten days. Bookmark the USCIS TPS page, check it religiously, and don’t get comfortable.

Question 1: Can I Hire a TPS Holder Right Now?

Yes — as long as their EAD is currently valid or covered by an active extension. A TPS-based work permit that hasn’t expired (or has been extended by a Federal Register notice or court order) is a perfectly acceptable List A document for Form I-9 purposes.

A few ground rules:

Don’t refuse to hire someone just because their EAD shows a TPS category code (A12 or C19). That’s national-origin and citizenship-status discrimination waiting to happen, and the USCIS Handbook for Employers guidance on avoiding discrimination makes clear the DOJ’s Immigrant and Employee Rights Section takes that seriously.

Check the actual expiration date — including any extended date from a court order or Federal Register notice — before assuming the document is stale.

Don’t demand extra documentation just because you know (or suspect) someone holds TPS. If the EAD is facially valid, treat it like any other valid List A document.

Question 2: Can I Keep My Current TPS Employees on Staff?

In most cases, yes — for now. Here’s the framework:

If the employee’s EAD is still within its printed or extended validity period, they remain authorized to work, full stop.

If a court order or Federal Register notice extended the EAD, that extension is legally binding until it’s undone — even if the underlying TPS designation has technically been “terminated” by DHS.

Don’t jump the gun. Several employers got burned earlier this year assuming an EAD had expired on a date DHS announced, only to have USCIS quietly push the date back days later. As one firm bluntly put it, don’t reverify before the current, operative expiration date — not the date you think should apply.

Question 3: When Do I Actually Have to Terminate a TPS Employee?

This is where things get real, and where you need to move carefully:

Reverification is required when the employee’s work authorization documentation actually expires — not before, and not based on rumors or headlines.

At reverification, the employee must present new, unexpired evidence of continued work authorization, following the USCIS handbook section on automatic extensions of employment authorization. An expired TPS-based EAD, once truly expired, doesn’t count.

If the employee can’t produce valid proof of continued authorization, federal law (INA § 274A) generally doesn’t let you keep them employed — continuing to do so can expose your company to liability.

Before you fire anyone, check whether they have another basis for work authorization. Plenty of TPS holders also have pending asylum applications, green card processes, or other status entirely independent of TPS. Don’t assume TPS is their only lifeline.

Apply the process consistently. If you’re reverifying TPS-based EADs from one country but not another, or treating similarly situated employees differently, you’re inviting a national-origin discrimination claim under INA § 274B.

Talk to immigration counsel before any adverse action. Given how fast this area is shifting, a termination that looked legally required on a Tuesday might look premature — or even discriminatory — by Friday.

Question 4: Documentation and Form I-9 Mechanics

The government’s own instructions have been refreshingly (if confusingly) specific here. For most of the countries still under active litigation, USCIS is telling employers to do the following on Form I-9:

In Section 1, enter “as per court order” for the expiration date field.

In Section 2, enter the current court-ordered extension date (these vary by country — see the table below) along with a note in the Additional Information box.

For E-Verify cases, use that same extended date.

Do not reverify using E-Verify — reverification always happens on paper, via Supplement B of Form I-9.

Employers may (but aren’t required to) attach the USCIS country-specific alert to the employee’s Form I-9 as supporting documentation.

Keep monitoring — these dates have moved multiple times already in 2026 (some countries had three different “release” updates between July 1 and July 17 alone).

Several countries got three different “release” updates in July alone as courts and USCIS traded punches, and as of July 24, 2026, no newer country-specific update has superseded the July 17 releases for Ethiopia, Yemen, Burma, Somalia, South Sudan, or Syria, or the July 10 release for Haiti. A Word on Venezuela — It’s Its Own Beast

Venezuela deserves special mention because its situation is more tangled than the rest. There are two separate TPS designations (2021 and 2023) with different termination dates and different litigation histories, and both have already been terminated. Practically, that breaks Venezuelan TPS employees into three buckets:

Category 1 — Protected through October 2, 2026: They received a qualifying EAD, I-797, or I-94 showing that expiration date, issued on or before February 5, 2025.

Category 2 — Possible 540-day auto-extension: They filed a timely EAD renewal with a receipt notice dated before February 6, 2025; whether the extension applies depends on the original card’s expiration date.

Category 3 — Authorization has lapsed: Everyone else. These employees are not authorized to work based on TPS alone, though they may have another basis for authorization worth checking before any action is taken.

Given how easily these categories can be confused (and how badly you don’t want to get this wrong), Venezuelan TPS cases are prime candidates for a quick call to counsel before you do anything on the I-9 front.

A Quick Note on the Litigation (Kept Brief, As Promised)

We won’t drag you through the whole legal saga, but here’s the headline: in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the TPS statute largely bars courts from reviewing DHS’s decisions to end a country’s designation, reversing lower court rulings that had found the Haiti termination was tainted by improper motives. That ruling didn’t instantly end TPS for every affected employee — it removed the primary legal shield that had been keeping several terminations on ice, and courts are now working through what that means case by case. Advocacy groups have been vocal that the human stakes are enormous — healthcare industry groups, for example, have flagged that thousands of Haitian nurses and home health aides could lose their jobs as this plays out. Whatever your view of the policy, the operational reality for HR is the same: the rules are actively in motion, and yesterday’s guidance might already be outdated.

Practical Takeaways

Check, don’t guess. Before taking any action — hiring, reverifying, or terminating — look up the current USCIS guidance for that specific country. Dates have changed multiple times per month this year.

Never reverify early. Wait until the actual, currently operative expiration date. Reverifying too soon (or demanding extra paperwork because someone is a TPS holder) risks a discrimination claim under INA § 274B.

Use the “as per court order” convention for Section 1 and the current extension date in Section 2 for countries still under active stays (currently Ethiopia, Yemen, Burma, Somalia, and South Sudan).

Treat Haiti and Syria as accelerated cases — Mullin cleared the path for their terminations to move forward, even though a residual court order is still technically extending some EADs as of the source releases reviewed here.

Handle Venezuela separately and carefully — sort employees into the three categories above before making any I-9 decision, and don’t assume October 2, 2026 applies to everyone.

Apply your process uniformly. Whatever reverification standard you apply to one TPS-based EAD, apply the same standard across the board, regardless of the employee’s country of origin.

Confirm alternate work authorization before terminating. Many TPS holders have another immigration status or pending application that independently authorizes their employment.

Loop in immigration counsel before taking adverse action based on TPS status — this is not the year to wing it.

Watch the broader TPS litigation, too, not just your eight focus countries. The July 21, 2026 order blocking OBBBA-related EAD cutoffs for Ukraine, El Salvador, and Sudan is a good reminder that new court rulings can pop up fast and touch employee populations you weren’t already tracking.

Subscribe to USCIS/E-Verify alerts so you’re not relying on secondhand news to catch the next update — sign up through E-Verify Alerts or keep the USCIS TPS page bookmarked.

This area will keep shifting, probably for the rest of the year. The safest posture for HR teams right now is a mix of vigilance and humility: verify every date against the current source before you act, and resist the urge to treat any single week’s headlines as the final word.

Gilroy, CA – On Sunday, July 19, over 250 community members of all ages and backgrounds gathered at San Ysidro Park to protest the planned ICE facility under construction in Gilroy. The strategic placement of the ICE detention center, located in the southern region of Santa Clara County in Northern California, would allow for an increase in immigration enforcement activity, threatening surrounding communities.

The four-mile march to the detention center construction site began with lively chants demanding “Legalization for all” and “Justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, and Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán,” the most recent lives lost at the hands of ICE agents. Two of these most recent martyrs were shot by ICE in cold blood. The community also stood in solidarity with fellow immigrant rights activists by calling for “Hands off Nadia Topete!” and repeated “Shut it down!” just mere feet from the entrance of the ICE site.

Kímberly Cortéz-Solorio, an organizer with the Community Service Organization (CSO) San José, shared that the county of Santa Clara and the state’s attorney general are engaged in legal proceedings against ICE which have temporarily halted the construction. But they reminded the community to “celebrate cautiously,” not let down their guard and to continue to demand a permanent halt.

The second CSO San José speaker, Ariya Amin, called out the hypocrisy of ICE, which labels people as “illegal,” while ICE agents regularly commit illegal atrocities with impunity. From planning the ICE facility in unincorporated Gilroy, to arresting people without warrants, to committing severe and daily human rights violations, ICE's actions have been unlawful. Amin declared that this administration has a duty to obey “the will of [the] people,” and reminded attendees that it is up to el pueblo to ensure that our consent is considered and prioritized.

The crowd also heard from Huy Tran, the executive director of Services, Immigrant Rights & Education Network (SIREN). During his speech, Tran asked the community to reflect on how well we hold accountable those in power and to remind them who is actually in charge here: the people. Tran stressed the importance of having difficult conversations, continuing the struggle, and letting others “see the activation” by being civically engaged.

Edwin Salazar from the Community Agency for Resources, Advocacy and Services asked the audience to imagine the implications of this ICE site and its proximity to beloved areas with high-immigrant populations, such as Gilroy and San José. Salazar shared how this country conditions its citizens via capitalism and urged the “community to collectivize” our resources to move forward.

Megan Sweet with Freedom Road Socialist Organization spoke about the acceleration of “large-scale invasions by the DHS” and how the brutality of operations we see on national news has already been witnessed in our streets. Sweet shared the cases of Ulises Peña López, who was left disabled after a violent encounter with ICE and ultimately deported, and Guillermo Medina Reyes, who was arrested by federal agents and is currently facing a legal battle.

Representing Working Partnerships USA, Rebeca Armendariz announced that the Santa Clara County Counsel (who had filed a lawsuit against ICE) had won their request for a temporary injunction, putting on pause any construction work for the coming weeks. Despite ICE not being prepared with the paperwork, Armendariz shared, the true threat was the mobilization of the masses.

In early September, the construction of this ICE detention center will resume and Gilroy organizers affirm they will be there to greet it. The struggle they are building will outpace and outlast anything ICE constructs.

text:
HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- It's been nearly three weeks since a man was shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on Canal Street.

The Department of Homeland Security, from the beginning, has said the ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo because he was trying to run over an agent.

Something his family and the other four men in his van that morning have disputed.

On Saturday, community members gathered to hold a procession and vigil for him in Magnolia Park as they seek the truth about what happened.

Community members told ABC13 it was about honoring Salgado Araujo as well as all the immigrants who have helped build communities throughout Houston.

Rows of yellow construction hats and dozens of people marching arm in arm. A sign of support from people across the community as they took to the streets of Magnolia Park on Sunday.

Salgado's family said he was an undocumented construction worker who was working to gain his legal status, adding that he had been in the United States for 35 years and had no criminal record.

"When we see Lorenzo, we see our fathers. We see our uncles. We see our brothers. We see our husbands. We see our fellow workers. We see our familia. DHS has said Salgado was never the target of their enforcement. But DHS says an ICE officer shot and killed him after he tried to run over an agent," said the executive director of the United Latino Ministry Methodist Church, Lydia Munoz.

The federal government said there is no body camera or dash camera video of the incident.

It's created an uproar from many in the community over the last three weeks, who demand transparency through this investigation.

text:
By John McNamara – nbpoliticus.com

NEW BRITAIN – Thumbs up and honking of horns from motorists were frequent on Saturday afternoon, July 25th, at the corner of Corbin Avenue and West Main Street at a “pop up” protest organized by Indivisible Greater New Britain.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero were killed during Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) involved car pursuits this month in Texas and Maine. New Britain area residents turned out for the “Justice for Johan and Lorenzo Stop ICE Now” rally, a protest that occurred in hundreds of communities on Saturday.

“We’re protesting against the abuses and the killings done by ICE,” said Mary-Joan Forstbauer of New Britain, a leader of Indivisible Greater New Britain. “Neighbors came out with signs and flags to say clearly: hate won’t make American great,” said organizers in a statement posted to Indivisible Greater New Britain’s Facebook page. “This country was built by immigrants, and we must end ICE abuses and demand dignity for every person.”

In New Britain, the Common Council previously adopted a resolution addressing “concerns related to federal immigration enforcement that have created uncertainty among some residents, potentially discouraging individuals from accessing essential city services or engaging with local institutions.”

The resolution states that “nothing in this resolution is intended to interfere with federal authority or require any city employee to act beyond the scope of their lawful duties.” The resolution, adopted amid widespread protests against federal ICE violence and human rights abuses last winter, reinforces Connecticut’s Trust Act first enacted in 2013 “to establish clear guidance about when state and local law enforcement would respond to requests from federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”) for information or assistance with ICE detainers” according to the CT Attorney General’s office. In 2025 and again this year the Legislature added more safeguards and by allowing individuals to sue ICE agents for disregarding due process and violating constitutional rights.

Indivisible Greater New Britain say it plans future direct action and advocacy against federal ICE abuses and in support of upholding the rule of law and due process rights. For more information email: indivisiblegreaternewbritain@gmail.com.

text:
A protest against the Immigration & Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency in downtown Nantucket on Saturday was marred by an alleged assault on a 69-year-old woman who was taking part in the demonstration.

The "Justice For All" protest, organized by the left-leaning political action group Indivisible Nantucket, began with a candlelight vigil at Children's Beach and was followed by a march through the downtown area.

The incident occurred as protestors were marching down South Beach Street, chanting and carrying signs. That was when a man in a blue blazer allegedly charged through the protest.

"As our group walked, a couple approached from the opposite direction," Indivisible Nantucket leader Alison Forsgren told the Current. "Rather than stepping aside onto Whaler's Lane to let us pass, they forced their way through the procession, shouting that we were 'crazy' among other things, and pushing participants. One woman was shoved but caught before she fell. Laura was knocked to the ground, landing on a pile of bricks and rubble at the corner of South Beach and Whaler's Lane. She was slow to get up and needed time to catch her breath."

The woman was island resident Laura Anderson, who has been a member of Indivisible Nantucket since 2017.

"I was silently walking with the group, holding a candle, when I heard a man yelling loudly and angrily," Anderson said in a statement shared with the Current. "Without any warning, he suddenly and forcefully pushed me from the rear. I had no chance to catch myself and fell hard onto a pile of bricks on the sidewalk. I had never spoken to him before, and I did nothing to provoke or threaten him. I couldn't get up on my own, and was frightened that more violence might follow. A police officer who was across the street responded almost immediately and began questioning the man."

Forsgren said Nantucket Police officers "immediately apprehended the man. He said he had no identification because his wife had left with his wallet."

Police have not yet responded to the Current's inquiry about the incident; however, the incident was noted in the department's public log as a "disturbance" and that a criminal complaint had been filed. The man's identity was not disclosed in the police log.

Anderson went to Nantucket Cottage Hospital on Sunday to be evaluated as a result of the incident.

"I went to the hospital because I was in pain and I wanted to make sure I hadn't suffered serious injuries," Anderson said. "I'm still recovering and continue to have pain both physically and emotionally. I participated in a peaceful vigil to stand against violence, and instead I became the victim of an unprovoked act of violence myself. No one should have to fear being assaulted simply for peacefully gathering with their community. I hope the person responsible is held accountable, and that no one else has to experience what I did."

Saturday's protest was the latest demonstration organized by Indivisible Nantucket, which has been the driving force behind numerous rallies against President Donald Trump's administration since he took office in 2024.

The "Justice For All" vigil and march on Saturday was organized to express "concern about ICE. It was part of a nationwide day of action supporting due process rights for everyone," Forsgren said.

United States President Donald Trump’s border czar says the vetting of an immigration officer involved in the deadly shooting of a Colombian native in Maine is under internal review after the officer’s relatives revealed to The Associated Press that he had a history of serious mental health struggles and violent behaviour.

Tom Homan said on Sunday that if the allegations against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer are true, “I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting.”

“There’s several things under review,” Homan said on CNN about the officer, Army veteran David Brouillette. “The training is under review. I know this specific case, as far as the vetting, is under review by the internal affairs section.”

Questions about the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) rush to hire, train and deploy thousands of new ICE officers to carry out Trump’s immigration crackdown have come into stark focus after back-to-back deadly shootings of immigrants in Maine and Houston.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ordered a pause in vehicle stops after the Maine shooting, but Trump almost immediately reversed course and insisted the stops resume as a necessary tool in his campaign to round up and deport immigrants without current legal status.

DHS did not immediately respond on Sunday to a request for comment about the internal review.

Homan said that “changes have been made” and that acting ICE director David Venturella has issued a new directive that body cameras must be in use if officers make a vehicle stop.

“Right now, on all vehicle stops, there’s at least one body camera on site to record the entire event,” he said.

He said Venturella “sent an instruction out that he wants at least one body camera on those vehicle stops, so we have everything on video”.

It is unclear if the steps the department is taking will be enough to quell the concerns coming from certain Congress lawmakers over DHS training and tactics as it tries to reach Trump’s mass deportation goals.

Lawmakers push for answers

Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns.

Democrats pressed ICE officials during a closed-door briefing for the House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee last week, leaving some with more questions than answers.

Lawmakers were told during the briefing that there have been 56 complaints of excessive force against ICE officers – 32 were cleared, and one was referred for disciplinary action.

No discipline had yet been handed out, the lawmakers said they were told. The rest of the incidents are still under investigation.

Meanwhile, Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has pushed for the use of body cameras and ensured funding for the effort. She had said it was “extremely unfortunate” that the officer involved in the shooting in her home state was not using a camera.
